utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the record, may we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour. Phillip Weiner for the Prosecution, with Sureta Chana, attorney David Re, and our trial manager, Ana Vrljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Peter Morrissey, appearing for Mr. Halilovic, with co-counsel, Mr. Mettraux, and our legal assistant, Mr. Cengic present in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halilovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. How was your stay in Sarajevo during your provisional release?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very good and very useful, owing to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Well, the Trial Chamber notes that the parties filed their final trial briefs on the 25th August. Following the motion to postpone closing arguments for one extra day filed by the Prosecution on the 26th August, the closing arguments were postponed for one day until today, because the Trial Chamber granted the motion in order to allow the parties additional time to prepare their response to opposing arguments submitted in the final briefs. At this stage, the Trial Chamber is seized with some motions filed by the parties. There are two of them that we should deal with before the closing arguments. The first one is a Defence notice concerning nature and the scope of the case presented in the Prosecution's final trial brief, filed on the 26th August. In its notice, the Defence alleged that the Prosecution final trial brief goes far beyond the pleadings of the indictment and the requests the Trial Chamber not to allow the Prosecution to go beyond pleadings as they exist in the indictment and to disregard submissions and arguments which go beyond that case. The Prosecution responded with a motion to strike the Defence notice filed on 29th August. The Trial Chamber is also seized of a motion for extension of pages filed by Defence on 25th of August, in which Defence seeks a 50-page extension of its final trial brief. The Prosecution filed a response to the late Defence motion for extension of pages on 26th August and a motion to strike Halilovic's final brief as an abuse of process on the 29th August. The Trial Chamber notes that the practice direction on the lengths of briefs and motions provided the Trial Chamber with the flexible mechanism to control the length and the format of filing of the parties. Clause (C)7 of the practice direction provides for the possibility of obtaining an authorisation from the Trial Chamber to exceed the page limits under exceptional circumstances. The Trial Chamber would like to hear the Defence as to the exceptional circumstances that necessitate the oversized filing. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the circumstances essentially are these, that this was an expert case with expert technical matters that had to be determined. But -- and in particular, because it's a command responsibility case, there were significant and very technical issues that arose as a result. The nature of the de jure case against Halilovic, the chains of subordination that existed between Halilovic and various other relevant bodies, the nature of the institution or the organisation which was said to be commanded by Halilovic, and the various indicators of that command are all matters which are amenable to technical analysis by applying military doctrine and by assessing that military doctrine with reference to the evidence of witnesses. The de jure -- just perhaps a few just so we're clear about how it's to be handled. The de jure case of the Prosecutor required analysis of particular meetings and particular orders. The Zenica meeting was pleaded in the indictment as an occasion of appointment. The role of Halilovic's Chief of Staff had to be explained and the powers that that role gave him had to be explained; the details of the order of the 30th of August, Exhibit D146, had to be explained; the implications of the map, Exhibit D131, had to be explained; the relevance and implications of particular orders on which the Prosecution relied, particularly Exhibit D161, the order of 2nd of September by Halilovic to Vahid Karavelic had to be explained; and other orders on which the Prosecution sought to base an inference of effective control had to be explained. All that had to be done in the absence of any expert evidence by the Prosecution, who did not seek to call an expert relevant to those questions, but instead tried to call and failed in succeeding in calling an expert who was going to explain about international humanitarian law, that being the British general, General Ridgway. Because of that, the Defence found it necessary, in order to discharge our duty of due diligence and competence, to provide an extensive analysis of those matters, and that was done in the brief. And for those reasons, we say this falls comfortably within the exceptional circumstances limb of that test on its own. A second reason is because the Defence says that there was a lack of specificity about certain parts of the Prosecution brief, and the Defence says that -- that we had to meet a range of arguments which the Prosecution did not ultimately persist with. In other words, we thought we had to meet arguments which ultimately did not materialise. An example of that is the argument that a prisoner of war at Uzdol was -- it was the subject of a charge, Mr. Slavko Mendic. Now, we prepared that, there's pages about that in the brief. We thought we had to meet that allegation. It turns out we didn't have to meet that allegation, and no one told us we didn't have to meet that allegation; we did a lot of work on that. The Prosecution led evidence from a man called Ramiz Delalic, the second-last Prosecution witness, that Halilovic and Zulfikar Alispago involved themselves in a cover-up, which involved a plan to kill those two young boys. Now, that doesn't feature in their brief, the closing brief. That's an argument that was dropped. But, however, the Defence had to meet that and we did meet it. We spent time on it. The Prosecution during argument alleged there was an operations group. We had to meet that, but you don't find that featuring in the Prosecution brief. The Prosecution have not withdrawn or did not withdraw paragraph 15 of the indictment, the allegation of actual notice by the Prosecution -- by Halilovic. But when you come to the final brief, they did not persist with that allegation. When it comes to the question of the law applicable to the -- to these offences, the Defence spent many pages on that. The Prosecution did not reveal what that applicable law was and they still haven't, even in the brief up to now. The nature of the failure to prevent in Grabovica -- sorry, the failure to punish the crime at Grabovica had changed utterly because now the argument is not that there was no investigation, as previously pleaded, but that the accused did next to nothing. In other words, there was a bad investigation. Further, the Defence had to guess and was unable to guess accurately all of the duties and the failures that the Prosecution was pleading. With respect to the duties and failures that the Prosecution alleges against Halilovic, they're articulated in part Roman numerals VIII of the Prosecution's final brief, and in that section it's evident that a list of things that Halilovic should have done is compiled. That list was not explained earlier on, though some parts are very anticipated in evidence, not all of it is. And so we say that those are the matters which raise the exceptional circumstances limb of this application. It's effectively technical evidence that we had to lead and it's also evidence in anticipation of arguments, the precise nature of which we could not be sure of. That's why we need the extra time and that's the exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that some of the arguments you have already put it on the Defence notice concerning the nature and scope of the case. Thank you. Mr. Weiner, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Re will respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, please be very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly will be, Your Honour. The Prosecution says that although the Defence may well have demonstrated that some reasons may exist to seek in advance in accordance with the practice direction an extension, what they have done in the circumstances is manifestly excessive -- it exceeds anything that could possibly be justified in the circumstances of this case, which as far as we know, apart from the contempt case, is the shortest trial to be heard before this Tribunal and probably will be the shortest trial to be heard before this Tribunal. What they have done, in effect, and if the Trial Chamber accedes, in our respectful submission, to allow the brief to be filed as is is to make a complete mockery of the procedures of the Tribunal, that is, the practice direction itself and the control by the Chambers of proceedings before them. My learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, has pointed to some things which may well justify seeking an extension for, we would respectfully submit, a small, a short -- we appreciate that 60.000 words or 200 pages is not a great amount of space, depending upon the length and complexity of the proceedings. Had we been asked, had the motion been put on before, our attitude would have been: Well, we don't object to an extension within reason. Now, within reason we would have said would have been maybe 10 to 15 per cent over, given the size and complexity of this particular trial in the context of the practice direction and why it exists. Now, what we have is we have seen basically something which is no more than an attempt to deceive the Trial Chamber. They have, as we've pointed out in our motion, crammed what appears to be about 158.000 words into 275 pages. That is something which is between two and a half and three times the amount or the -- the word limit in the practice direction. Now, saying that this case raises some issues just does not demonstrate exceptional circumstances, especially retrospectively. The submission my colleague made about Mr. Mendes would be laughable if the matter weren't so serious in terms of the wanton disregard of the practice direction of the Tribunal. Looking through the brief, there are three pages specifically devoted to Mr. Mendes, pages 16 to 19. That could not justify 98.000 words in addition of the word limited -- word limit mandated by the practice direction. Nothing could possibly justify that. The issues about the expert are also, in our submission, quite irrelevant. We didn't call an expert because the Defence opposed us calling an expert. The issues -- the expert issues of military law are no more complex in this issue -- in this case than in any other case, and this case is one of the least complex. There is one accused, two crime base incidents, and one count. It just pales in significance with almost every other case that is currently before this Tribunal or has been actually ever heard by this Tribunal. What is of great concern to the Prosecution if the Defence is allowed to get away with this is the methods which have been employed. Not only have they breached the wording of the practice direction, seven specific violations we have pointed out in our motion to strike it, but it's the manner of deception employed to file it and to file almost as an afterthought a one-line glib and meaningless throw-away explanation seeking an extension at the time of filing of the thing. Presented as a fait accomplis to the Trial Chamber it shows the grossest professional disrespect to the Office of the Prosecutor who has to respond to this almost -- or 500-page plus document between Friday morning, midmorning when we received it and Monday, which is yesterday, when we were supposed to respond to it. It showed the grossest disrespect to the Trial Chamber, the grossest disrespect to the Tribunal and the rules of the Tribunal, the grossest professional disrespect to the legal officers in Chambers who have to try and read this massive tome over the weekend to provide Your Honours with advice so Your Honours can hear it this morning. And it's not just the length; it's the way it's been done. The margins have been moved to the side. A special font has been used in the footnotes, so it's gone from 10 to 8 so it's virtually unreadable. And as we have pointed out, there are three particular pages, page 92, for example, contains over 1400 words. Now, if the Defence were honest about this, they would have come to Your Honours last week. This didn't come up suddenly. They just didn't suddenly realise that they were two and a half to three times over the word limit. They knew this, which is why the font size has been changed. It's why there are no numbers on the annex at the back. Which is why the index at the front has a different numbering system. It's why it has 254, and they have asked for extra pages to make it like as if they are trying to fit in with what they have instead of the 500-plus pages. Now had they come to the Trial Chamber this time last week with a genuine motion saying, Look, we're in trouble, Your Honours, we need more space, not 10 per cent, not 15 per cent, but 250 to 300 per cent. What would our reaction have been? And more importantly, what would Your Honours' reaction have been? I think everyone knows what the reaction of the Trial Chamber would have been. It probably would have been -- and I'm not second-guessing Your Honours in any way or being disrespectful, but probably to allow in the give and take of this particular trial -- and within the flexibility granted by the practice direction, some leeway, not two and a half times to three times the leeway. What has been filed is basically oppressive. It's oppressive to the other side, it's oppressive to Chambers, and it's oppressive to the Trial Chamber. Now, of course we don't object to the Defence filing a final trial brief, but our submission is in its present form it cannot be accepted, it should be stricken, and they should be made to re-file it in accordance with the practice direction. And if Your Honours are minded to accede to a small variation, we won't object to a small variation. But had we would known about this a week ago, our opposition would have -- it would have given us time to prepare our own brief which raises the issue, of course, of equality of arms. Had we known they wanted so much, why couldn't we come before the Trial Chamber and say, Well, look, the issues are a bit complex we'd like a bit extra as well. It's been done in such a sneaky, deceptive and underhanded way that the Trial Chamber cannot countenance this sort of behaviour by Defence counsel. In my respectful submission it is -- in the Prosecution's respectful submission, it is excessive and it should be stricken. If Your Honours wish me to address the other one, I can, the other motion, or I can come to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very, very briefly. Maybe two or three sentences, because we have received your motion on that issue already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes, this second motion -- well, if it is in fact a motion. It is called a Defence notice. As we have pointed out, apart from the fact that it raises issues which are res judicata between the parties, that is, namely the issues of pleadings and particulars which we will address in our closing submissions at a later point, it is no more than an attempt to extend the 500-plus pages, in reality, that they have filed by another 14 pages. This time, as you can see, I mean the contrast is quite stark because the font is actually readable on the -- in the footnotes. It only raises additional argument which should have been in the final trial brief in anticipation. Because there is nothing in our final trial brief which was not pleaded in the indictment, not in the -- not in the pre-trial brief, not in the opening, and certainly not in evidence. Our final trial brief is based upon the combination of all four, as one would expect, after hearing a trial which has gone for some six months or so. And the reason, we say, this ploy has been employed was because if the Defence were to read on to the record the 14 pages of additional argument, which is probably some 10.000 words or so, it would take them 40 to 45 minutes, the averaging reading time of about three minutes per page, and it would cut into their oral submission time. It is nothing more than yet another ploy to try and gain an unfair, sneaky, underhand advantage over the Prosecution in the argument of the final trial brief. It should be stricken from the record, and if the Defence wish to make these oral arguments, they are quite welcome to do so. And they should use their time and use some discipline in the same way that we have as all other parties in all other matters before the Tribunal should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, having considered the arguments presented by both parties in their written and oral submissions, the Trial Chamber grants a 50-page extension of the Defence trial -- final trial brief because the Trial Chamber finds the exceptional circumstances in the present case, in particular the complexity of the evidence presented in the court as well as recent decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber, justifies the extension. However, the Trial Chamber observes that the Defence final brief is not formatted as required by the directive and exceeds the page limits of 200 pages as provided for in the directive by more than 50 pages if formatted as required by the directive. The Trial Chamber therefore requests the Defence to re-file its final trial brief, which must not exceed a 50-page extension and which respects the formatting set out in the directive, in particular in clause (A). The brief shall be re-filed in a redacted version no later than Friday, 2nd of September, without any additions, by deleting, where possible, parts of the draft, such as those of the repetitive nature or lengthy quotations. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's just one thing I wanted to clarify and that is the annexes. I didn't address that. Our argument is that 15 pages of annexes are actually part of the brief. Is that encompassed in Your Honours' -- in the Trial Chamber's ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe everything should be included in the 250 pages altogether. As for the Defence notice concerning the nature and scope of the case presented in the Prosecution's final trial brief as well as the motion filed by the Prosecution to strike the Defence notice filed on the 29th August, after due consideration of the arguments of both parties, the Trial Chamber first notes its decision on Defence motion for striking out paragraphs in Prosecution pre-trial brief issued on 7th February 2005. The Trial Chamber reiterates, as stated in its decision and during the pre-trial conference, that it will base its finding on what has been pleaded in the indictment. The Trial Chamber further notes that in the Defence notice the Defence submits what it considers to be the Prosecution's case based on the indictment and the Prosecution pre-trial brief. The Trial Chamber finds that those submissions could have been included into the Defence final trial brief or that in any case they can be raised by the Defence during their closing arguments. The Trial Chamber therefore declines to consider the Defence notice. It is so decided. Well, let's come to the closing argument. Mr. Weiner, are you ready to deliver it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Chana will start. The three counsel will each argue. Ms. Chana will go first, then I will argue, then Attorney Re will argue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to remind you that you have three and a half hours to deliver it, no matter how do you divide your labour in your team, that's your matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We divided it with a scalpel, with precision, and we will stick to the three and a half hours, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the earlier, the better. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. The Prosecution's closing arguments are set out in the Prosecution's final trial brief. And it is of course unnecessary for me to repeat all of these arguments orally. Our purpose today, Your Honours, is to give an oral response to the arguments contained in the Defence final trial brief. Having said that, it has become clear to us that in the time available for oral arguments today, that we will really not be -- it will not be possible for us to even address all the arguments that have been raised in the Defence closing brief. Your Honours, we've just discussed the brief. Your Honours have already ruled on the motion. It has contained some extremely dense footnotes, and my eyes, which were not as young as they were, have found it very difficult to read them. But nevertheless, by the standards of this international criminal tribunal, this is really what we considered a smallish-to-medium case. And therefore, the need for such a long trial brief is, in those circumstances, difficult to understand. In our respectful submission, Your Honours, the Defence brief is a case of not seeing the wood through the trees. It is of such great length because it sets out a detailed description of each branch of each tree but fails to describe the forest as a whole. In oral arguments today, Your Honours, I propose to deal with the broader picture. Now, the broader picture begins with the question as to why this Prosecution was brought. It was brought because innocent civilians, over 63 in number, were killed by members of the armed forces of the ABiH, in violation of the most basic principles of international humanitarian law. The youngest victim was a girl called Mladenka Zadro, a girl a few weeks shy of her fourth birthday. The oldest victim is a Marko Maric, an 87-year-old man. This is why we are here today. This prosecution is about justice for victims. When we descend into the detailed minutiae of the evidence, we might argue about whether it has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt that a particular victim was in fact killed by members of the ABiH, or whether the killer really knew of their status as innocent victims. The Defence has argued at some length, and my colleague Mr. Weiner will be addressing the crime base evidence a little later. But, at the outset, one point must be emphasised, which is this: Even if the Trial Chamber were to accept that the Prosecution case has not been proved in relation to every single one of the alleged victims, it is clear that certain innocent civilians were killed by the soldiers of the ABiH. I need only refer, for instance, to paragraph 110 of the Defence brief, where it is conceded that the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that six of the victims in Grabovica were murdered by members of the ABiH, and that in respect of at least four victims, members of the 9th Motorised Brigade took part in the killing. As is indicated in paragraph 96 of the Defence brief, these victims that the Defence has conceded included an old couple, Pero Maric and his wife, Dragica. Pero was shot in the head outside his home in the presence of ABiH soldiers, who were eating and drinking. His invalid wife, who was inside the home at the time, knew that he had been shot and lay in bed for hours later, hearing the soldiers drinking and eating outside her house, knowing that the soldiers would eventually come to kill her, which they did. The incident cannot be characterised as anything other than an atrocity of war. I do not understand the Defence to in any way argue to the contrary. It was to punish this type of wartime atrocity, to prevent their recurrence in the future, to bring justice to the memory of the victims that the Tribunal was set up. In paragraph 80, the Defence brief asserts that, and I quote: "The identification of the alleged perpetrators is therefore of critical importance in establishing the accused's effective control over that person." A proposition to which of course we agree. Yet remarkably in paragraph 81, the Defence allege a failure to identify the perpetrators and go on to allege it could either amount to or be relevant to an abuse of process -- application. This is particularly difficult to understand, given that the Defence has conceded the death of at least six innocent civilians at the hands of the ABiH, and at least four of them at the hands of the 9th Brigade. This allegation against the Prosecution might in itself be regarded as an abuse of process. The innuendo is therefore clear, Your Honours, that killing of even these conceded murders appears to the Defence as simply to be not enough. This clearly cannot be said to be a credible and responsible argument on the part of the Defence. The Prosecution would like to make it clear that the death of even one civilian is one too many, attracts criminal responsibility, and is definitely a war crime. We cannot be lulled into this kind of moral anaesthesia. Your Honours, this is solely a command responsibility case brought under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The simple issues before the Trial Chamber are whether the accused was the commander of the soldiers and had effective control over the perpetrators who committed these crimes. This is the sole test, and both the Defence and the Prosecution are happily in agreement in this regard. Excuse me, Your Honours. And if he was, whether or not the accused took the necessary steps to prevent the commission of these crimes or to punish the perpetrators thereof. The evidence to prove this can either be direct or circumstantial. Again, both parties are in agreement here. Despite the simplicity of these issues, the Defence brief raises all sorts of arguments which are of no apparent relevance and also of no possible merit. Again, time constraints prevent me from identifying them all, but if I can begin at the first paragraph of the Defence brief to give a few examples. The very first paragraph of the Defence brief complains that the Prosecution did not plead in the indictment whether the armed conflict in question was international or non-international in character. This is of course immaterial. The accused is charged with a single count of murder under Common Article 3. It is now well-established law -- case law of the Tribunal -- it is trite law that the Common Article 3 applies to both international and non-international armed conflicts. So there is no need for Your Honours or for us, indeed, to specify this in this indictment. Your Honours can look forward to Mr. Re, who will be expounding on this aspect of the law later on in his arguments. What is more -- even more difficult to understand is how the Defence can plead in a final trial brief that the indictment was inadequately pleaded. Indeed in the very first footnote the Defence argues that the rights of the accused have been violated by this inadequate pleading. However, as the footnote goes on to acknowledge, the Trial Chamber has already ruled on the Defence motion raising these very issues, as Your Honours ruled this morning as well. So therefore, it has definitely been dealt with, and there is no basis for the Defence to raise it again at this stage. In paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Defence brief then go on to suggest that the Prosecution has not proved there was an armed conflict at the relevant place and time. This argument is particularly difficult to understand, and to that end I refer to the April 22nd motion on agreed facts filed by the parties for the fact there was an armed conflict is abundantly obvious from those facts. The suggestion that there may have been no armed conflict also seems directly contrary to other submissions in the Defence brief; for instance, paragraph 218 which states that: "There has been combat activity in the Prozor, Jablanica, and Mostar regions for months." Even if there was, for instance, no fighting actually occurring in Grabovica at the time of the crimes, this does not mean then there was no armed conflict in the area at the time. The soldiers who committed the crime were clearly engaged in armed conflict, even if they were not fighting the enemy at that particular moment. In Uzdol, of course, there was an armed conflict which has not been seriously denied by the Defence in their brief. Paragraphs 7 and 8 of the Defence brief and the accompanying footnote then makes rather -- makes a rather extraordinary submission. Here the Defence argues that the underlying crimes might have been random or isolated acts, in which case they would not qualify as war crimes. This submission is of course contrary to the most basic principles of international criminal law. An isolated or random act might not qualify as a crime against humanity or genocide, but it can certainly be a war crime. If a soldier on his own or her own initiative kills a single protected person, that is a war crime and the soldier's superior has the responsibility to punish for it. At paragraph 46, the Defence asks the Chamber to consider the civilians in Uzdol as levee en masse. While it is the correct legal position that when civilians spontaneously take up arms in defence of invading troops, they are said to constitute a levee en masse and can be regarded as combatants for the purposes of the laws of war, but this is only so if the armed forces have not been formed or have not asserted their military authority over the area. The Defence brief makes numerous references to the HVO and their military presence in Uzdol. The law is very clear that there cannot be civilians and soldiers fighting together and then assert the civilian side is levee en masse. This is not the correct position in law. Another example, Your Honour, is at paragraph 331 there is yet another extraordinary claim in that the Prosecution case is a de jure case only, and the issues of effective control must be limited to the scenario where the Trial Chamber makes a finding that Halilovic was the de jure commander of the 9th and 10th Brigades. This is an incorrect position, as the Prosecution case has always been that the accused demonstrated both de facto and de jure authority. The indictment at paragraph 39 clearly states: "Sefer Halilovic," and I quote, "demonstrated both formal de jure and de facto power, by his command and control in military matters in a matter -- in a manner consistent with the exercise of superior authority, by issuing orders, instructions, and directives to the units, by ensuring the implementation of these orders, instructions, and directives, and bearing full responsibility for their implementation." In fact all our pleadings, pre-trial brief, opening statement, we have consistently maintained this position. A huge section of the Defence brief is similarly devoted to the duties of a Chief of Staff, which are not denied and they are correctly stated, but it has never been our case that the accused was in Herzegovina within his duties and capacity as Chief of Staff. The accused went to Herzegovina to command Operation Neretva by the authority of Commander Delic. That is our position. Your Honours, time does not permit me to deal with the numerous other immaterial and/or erroneous arguments advanced by the Defence in their final trial brief. The Defence brief also complains -- and much has been made of the fact that the Prosecution did not call certain witnesses, yet called other witnesses. It is called prosecutorial discretion. For instance, they complain that commander Rasim Delic, who was, as they put it, "renounced to be called." Clearly, the Prosecution cannot call every witness they interviewed. There is a clear policy at this Tribunal to shorten cases, a policy, I may add, which was actively encouraged by the Chamber, that the Prosecution only call witnesses or as many witnesses as they need to prove the case for the Prosecution to the required standard of proof, which is what the Prosecution did. Your Honours, the Defence has made much of this, this aspect of us not calling witnesses, but it must not be lost that the Defence had full disclosure of all the witness statements, and they themselves were at liberty to call any witnesses they felt would further their case from the Prosecution witnesses we did not call. They could have subpoenaed them or asked the Chamber to do so. Having not done so, the Defence suggests that this failure to call every witness on the initial witness list should somehow result in inferences being drawn that are favourable to the accused. This may be convenient for the Defence, but we invite this Honourable Chamber not to draw such positive inferences, given our Prosecution witness list. We also point out that the Defence equally did not call the witnesses they had on their witness list. The Defence had every opportunity to present their case and call any witnesses they desired. They were on notice as to who they were. Your Honours, the Defence also make much of the fact that Ramiz Delalic, the deputy commander of the 9th Brigade, was called to give evidence. Your Honour, it's important to note the only reason the Prosecution was -- had brought Ramiz Delalic to testify here is because the accused himself took him to Herzegovina for Operation Neretva. It is not possible to address all these arguments, nor is it even possible to respond orally to each of the Defence arguments. Your Honours, to a significant degree the final trial brief of the parties must be left to speak for themselves; however, in the time available for oral argument today, a few salient points can be emphasised. The first point relates to the nature of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the relevant time. I think it's fairly common ground between the Prosecution and the Defence that it was a fairly disorganised and undisciplined army at the time. When the conflict broke out in the former Yugoslavia, Bosnian Muslims were originally together with the Bosnian Croats fighting against the Bosnian Serbs. Bosnian Muslims at that stage were often fighting under the auspices of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat army. The ABiH was only formed in late 1992 out of units of the Territorial Defence, the TO. At the times material to the indictment, it was still a force, if you will forgive the use of a vernacular expression, held together by spit. The Defence has at some length highlighted its problems of discipline, coordination, and resources. The Defence goes so far as to suggest that in view of this disorganisation and lack of discipline within the ABiH forces, there was not even an armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina within the legal definition of that expression. The Defence suggest at paragraph 3 of their brief that there were at the most "localised hostilities or skirmishes." The Prosecution submits that this Defence submission cannot be seriously entertained. Despite all the problems of coordination and discipline in the ABiH, there can be no doubt at the time that it was a single army. It had laws which regulated the conduct of the army, it had a supreme command, it had six corps, it had the military security, it had weaponry and formal structures for discipline. It had a status as an army within the national and international arenas. As to the definition of an armed conflict, the Appeals Chamber said in the Tadic jurisdiction appeal that "an armed conflict exists where there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state." We submit that there can be no doubt on the evidence that the ABiH was either a governmental authority or an organised armed group within the meaning of that definition, and in numerous other cases before the Tribunal concerning crimes committed within the same time frame, it has been held and accepted that the ABiH satisfies this definition. However, another theme of the Defence appears to be is to suggest that because of the disorganisation and chaos within the ABiH, no one was in effective control. Or at least, the suggestion is that the accused was not in effective control. The Prosecution submits that the Defence argument puts in issue a very important principle of international humanitarian law the very purpose of the legal principle of superior responsibility under Article 7(3) is to ensure that discipline will be maintained over members of the armed forces by their superiors. Armed forces have a duty to remain disciplined forces. The very purpose of international humanitarian law would be defeated if superiors would say that because their armed force was too disorganised and undisciplined, they are absolved of any responsibility for taking steps to ensure that crimes by their subordinates are prevented or punished under Article 7(3). Disorganised and undisciplined armies is a very thing that the principle of superior responsibility is designed to prevent. As I have said, Your Honours, it must be accepted that the ABiH fell within the definition of an organised armed group, as that expression was used by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdiction case. If the ABiH was an organised armed group, there must by definition have been some command structure responsible for commanding the group, upon whom the responsibilities of Article (3) would fall. The issue in this case was whether the accused fell within that command structure, and if so, whether or not he discharged the responsibilities that 7(3) imposed upon him. Ultimately, the Defence final trial brief acknowledge -- acknowledges that this is the issue. Paragraph 268 to 276 of the Defence brief suggests that it was Commander Delic who was in command of Operation Neretva 93. So the Defence is not really seriously denying that the chain of command over the operation extended to the top of the ABiH military hierarchy. The question is whether the accused was part of that chain. As to the question of who was responsible -- who the responsible commanders were, for the ABiH forces who committed the crimes in this case, it has been acknowledged in the case law of the Tribunal that the case of disorganised and newly formed forces, it can be sometimes difficult to tell. As the Trial Chamber said in the Celebici case with reference to the Bosnian Muslim forces at a somewhat earlier time: "The requirement of the existence of a superior subordinate relationship is particularly problematic in situations such as that of the former Yugoslavia during the period relevant to the present case - situations where previously existing formal structures have broken down and where, during an interim period, the new, possibly improvised, control and command structures, may be ambiguous and ill-defined ... Persons effectively in command of such more informal structures, with power to prevent and punish the crimes of persons who are in fact under their control, may under certain circumstances be held responsible for their failure to do so." In such circumstances where an armed forces is in a state of some disorganisation, the distinction between de jure and de facto authority may become blurred. It may not be clear what are the proper and authorised procedures for conferring command authority on a particular person. Accordingly, where a person has in fact been given authority to command, it may not be clear whether the authority is a legally and duly conferred de jure authority or whether it is a de facto authority. However, as the case law of the Tribunal indicates, it is not necessary to draw fine distinctions or undertake a close examination of military procedures for conferring command authority, since the case law of the Tribunal establishes firmly that superior responsibility, excuse me, under Article 7(3) attaches to both de jure and de facto superiors. The failure to recognise this is, in the Prosecution's submission, a major flaw in the Defence final trial brief. The Defence brief gives a separate treatment to the issue of de jure responsibility and to de facto responsibility. The Defence final brief deals with the issue of de jure authority in paragraphs 197 to 313. In these paragraphs, the Defence rely -- rely to a heavy degree on formal structures, formal military doctrines, and formal procedures that, according to the Defence, would have had to have been followed for de jure authority to have been conferred if the ABiH was operating by the book. There is a lengthy dissection in minute detail of the Delic order of 30th August 1993 and the meaning of the word "rukovodjenje" in B/C/S in a military context. There are arguments - I refer, for instance, at paragraphs 244 and 252 of the Defence brief - to the effect that the accused could only have been appointed commander by a specific order. At paragraphs 251 to 254 of the Defence brief there is discussion of the fact that the Prosecution has not established that an operation group was indeed in place at the time. However, Your Honours, all this means very little in a situation where the ABiH was not operating by the book or in strict compliance, as it were, with formal military procedures. The situation is described in paragraph 218 of the Defence brief in the words of the Defence. It says: "The ABiH had an immature command structure and few trained officers." As the Defence says in the same paragraph, the ABiH was uncoordinated, there was a gathering crisis in the areas of the 4th and 6th Corps, and the situation in Mostar was desperate. As I described it earlier, the ABiH was at that time an armed forces loosely held together. So in determining whether command authority had or had not been conferred on a given person in a such situation, the question can hardly be answered by reference to formal military doctrines and procedures, as the Defence would have us believe. Rather, it is the reality of the case which must be taken into account rather than abstract military theory which needs to be addressed. The evidence which we adduced at trial refers to the reality on the ground at the time of Operation Neretva and not some academic military theory. The Defence brief then finally goes to consider the issue of de facto authority at paragraphs 314 to 400. The Defence arguments are very lengthy but are neatly summarised in paragraph 314 of their brief. Here it is stated that the accused had no de facto command authority because of the poor state of command and control in the ABiH, the pattern of hostility to the accused, the insubordinate nature of the 9th Brigade troops, and the lack of a clear and comprehensible chain of command in the combat region. Yet, they conveniently rely on this non-existent chain of command going directly up to Delic -- Commander Delic, excuse me. While it has to be said that each of these four matters referred to in the Defence brief, if they were valid, would apply equally to de jure authority as much as to he de facto authority. As I have said, the very purpose of the doctrine of superior responsibility is to ensure that armed forces are disciplined. Whether commanders are appointed on a de jure basis or a de facto basis, commanders are commanders, and they have the duty to maintain discipline within their forces, either by preventing the crimes by their subordinates in the first place, or where that is not possible, by punishing them after the event. It would be absurd if it were a defence for a commander to say, I had no duty to maintain discipline because my subordinates were too indisciplined. Yet, the evidence does disclose the accused requested for these very same indisciplined forces to come to Herzegovina for combat operations. He can hardly then be heard to say they were too indisciplined and he had no effective control over them, which appears to be the Defence argument. So therefore, Your Honours, the question is not whether the formal military procedures were or were not followed in conferring command authority on the accused or how well organised and disciplined the ABiH was or was not at the time. The question is simply whether or not the accused was in a position of command authority. The Defence expressly agreed that the existence of a de jure command authority can also be established by inference. This is at the Defence brief paragraph 243. The same is true of de facto authority. At paragraph 165, they correctly state that whether the command authority is de facto or de jure, the test is one of effective control. At paragraphs 186 to 195, the Defence state that effective control is "not the same as appearance thereof" and not the same as "influence." The Prosecution accepts that the mere fact of appearance of command authority and the accused's influence may not of themselves be sufficient to prove command responsibility. However, the Defence has also conceded that the existence of command authority can be proved circumstantially, as Your Honour Liu very wisely advised us during trial, it is built step by step. When looking at the case as a whole, these factors of influence and seniority all go towards proof of his command responsibility by way of circumstantial evidence. The accused, Your Honours, was the most senior man in the area. Salko Gusic, the commander of the 6th Corps, stated, and it's -- I will quote just a short piece of his testimony because it is rather illustrative. "The Chief of Staff of the supreme command, he was a superior officer and we treated him as a superior officer. So it was not just a title, just a post. It carried authority with it, authority which we respected ... I can't say it fully replaced rank because rank carries some other defining elements, but as far as relations in the army went, it fully replaced ranks. When it came to duties, assignments, and so on, the functions -- or rather, the post, such as a chief, assistant, a deputy, and so on, fully replaced ranks ... It means a lot, sir. It means a lot. He was the second man in the army, the second-ranking general in the army. That means a lot. The number-two man. It still means a lot today." He went on to say: "What was the reality on the ground was that General Halilovic was the real authority there and those units there did not need a written order to enable him to engage them." That was the reality on the ground. You cannot look at specific military doctrine, things were not done by the book, it is how it was exercised at the time. Your Honour, Commander Delic was not present in Herzegovina, as he was based in Sarajevo. The background is clear. There was a seat in Sarajevo as well as a seat in Mostar, so everybody was extremely busy. Journalist Hodzic who was shadowing him during the war and who the Defence have agreed is an extremely credible witness stated in his evidence, and I quote, Your Honours: "He," the accused, "turned to Dr. Cibo and myself -- or rather, he said to Cibo, 'Cibo, tell Delic that I don't need him here. I'm preparing for the offensive and I don't need him interfering with things here.'" The accused was clearly in charge in Herzegovina and not Delic. The question then there is, Your Honours, whether on all the evidence, the only reasonable inference was the accused had command authority over the perpetrators of the crimes with which he is charged, either de facto or de jure. What does the evidence establish? After the Zenica meeting, senior commanders of the ABiH discuss future combat operations to be undertaken. At some point it was decided to launch Operation Neretva to free the corridor to Mostar. Commander Delic appointed the accused by the August 30th order to lead and command these operations. Your Honour, we'll come to the interpretation in a minute. To that end a forward command post was set up in Jablanica from where this operation was to be commanded. Your Honours, all the evidence is detailed in our Prosecution brief and time does not permit me to go into the evidence in any detail. Your Honours, the 30th August order is but one piece of evidence which has generated a lot of debate and I think we all know it by heart now. When it comes to the August 30th order, which is the Delic order, I raise the query as to how relevant the translation is to effective control. What does "rukovodjenje" mean? We've had many translations. Lead, control. That cannot -- it's but one piece of evidence. Your Honour, what is clear from this order is that the order gave the accused powers to lead the operation -- it certainly gave him orders to issue orders. He only had to consult Delic in case of more drastic proposals and solutions. He asked him, and it's significant when he says, in keeping with his authority, in keeping with the accused's authority, to solve problems in the field by issuing orders and the accused only had to report back to him on the orders that he issued. He did not need to get his permission before. The Prosecution has adduced evidence as to what this order meant to the many witnesses who gave their evidence here, and according to them this order gave Halilovic command authority over Operation Neretva. They considered him to be the commander. Your Honours, Witness Karavelic, he commander of the 1st Corps and a very senior member of the ABiH, and his evidence has been referred to in the Defence brief where it says -- he has often been quoted. He is quoted twice in the Defence brief as saying that he was unable to obey the order of Halilovic of resubordination of troops without prior reference to Delic. But Witness Karavelic stated and clarified that the only reason he asked Delic if he ought to obey the order requesting for the troops to go to Herzegovina was because he was not aware of the 30th August order. He made it very clear in his evidence that if he had known about the order, he would have obeyed the order given by Halilovic without recourse to Commander Delic. Witness Bakir Alispahic equally stated he was told by the accused that he was commanding the military operation in respect of this order. Jasarevic testified that this particular order gave Halilovic the power to issue commands on the spot and they would be obeyed. Your Honour, what was the accused's understanding of this order? Paragraph 258 states that the accused's understanding was that his role was one of coordination. Your Honour, the inspection team report which the accused filed on 20th September is illustrative on this point. I would like P -- D130 to be put on to the ELMO, Your Honour, if we can just have a look at it. Sorry I did not give enough notice for that. This, Your Honour, is the report filed by the inspection team members on 20th September, and it has been signed by the accused. Your Honour, it actually refers, if you look at the first page -- I'm not sure where -- yes. Let's start where it says -- it's strictly confidential, Sarajevo, 20th September, 1993. And this actually tells us what the accused understood what that August 30th order meant to him. And -- because it refers to it at the beginning. And it says: "With the approval of 29th August, 1993, from the commander of the SVK in his strictly confidential order dated 02/1647-1 dated 30th August, 1993, an expert team commission was established in order to coordinate combat operations and to carry out all other tasks in the zone of responsibility, et cetera." Your Honour, I would take you to the -- it details the people who were meant to be -- form part of this inspection team. It says: "The team went to the field on 29th August 1993 and was on mission until 19th September 1993." Your Honour, I will -- to save time, I'll skip it and in the middle of the paragraph where it says why did they go there? "With the aim of coordinating and executing combat operations," the word "executing," "an IKM, forward command post, was set up in Jablanica." Your Honour, it's important to note here that the Defence in their Defence brief at paragraph 264 deny that there was ever an existence of an IKM, and they say that the witnesses who testified to the existence of an IKM in Jablanica were labouring under a mistaken belief. It was the belief obviously shared by the accused because this is the very document that the accused signed as head of the inspection team. So what kind of words do they have there? So it was to execute combat operations. The forward command post was set up in Jablanica where the team planned the operation which covered the wide front from Gornji Vakuf to Mostar. Then in paragraph 1 it says "to estimate the combat readiness of the commands of the unit and to lead combat operations." Your Honour, it's instructive that the Bosnian translation equally says "rukovodjenje," the same as it says here. So whatever the translation which is accepted. Then it -- I'll go to the end of that paragraph where it says: "To implement the planned operation in the Neretva and Vrbas valley." So we have the words "implement the planned operation." Your Honour, this gives us a -- this document gives us a bit of an insight as to how the accused understood his own role in Operation Neretva. These words cannot be explained in a military doctrinal way; it's in the ordinary meanings of the word "lead," "execute." Your Honours, the Prosecution has produced many orders which were issued by the accused to give effect to Operation Neretva, and orders by other commanders engaged in this operation who issued orders based on the accused orders. All these orders are detailed in our Prosecution final brief and the documents speak for themselves. The Defence in their final brief suggest that many of the orders by the accused were not obeyed, which indicates lack of control by the accused. The mere fact that an order is not obeyed is not indicative of a lack of effective control. As long as sanctions exist for this disobedience and a commander had a material to enforce these sanctions, that would be sufficient. The Defence has also tried to suggest that all the orders which were issued by the accused and which were not consistent with his duties and inspection team member, for example, combat orders, resubordination orders, they were all consistent with command, were in fact emergency orders. This is an unconvincing argument, Your Honours, for orders they cannot explain away, and those are considered emergency. Or for other orders, like the Pasalic orders, which clearly resubordinates troops to the accused. The argument there is that these are not genuine documents. Your Honour, in respect of the MUP at paragraph 113 there is the assertion by the Defence that they were -- the accused was not in charge of the MUP forces who took part in combat. The minister, Alispahic, was very clear that although the MUP had a separate chain of command, in combat according to a well-established military doctrine of the doctrine of unifying command, that all troops and battle are under the command of the commander who's commanding the operation. It cannot be held otherwise. It would create havoc on the combat operation. Therefore, Your Honours, on the issue of command responsibility the Prosecution accepts that it has the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was the superior of the perpetrators of the underlying crimes. However, in determining whether the Prosecution has discharged its burden, it is necessary to look at the evidence as a whole. Each individual item of evidence has been minutely examined, but if an individual item of evidence is viewed in isolation, it may be capable of different interpretations which ought to be disregarded. All the evidence adduced in this case viewed as a whole, the only reasonable inference which can be drawn from this evidence is that the accused was the commander of Operation Neretva and the superior of -- superior of the perpetrators who committed the crimes. And the Prosecution invites the Trial Chamber to so hold. Your Honours, I'll now invite the Court to invite Mr. Weiner to take up the submissions from this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be addressing issues relating to Grabovica and Uzdol. In terms of Grabovica, I will discuss who was killed and by whom. On September 8th, 1993, soldiers from the 9th Motorised Brigade arrived in Grabovica. What was a quiet, peaceful village suddenly changed. Within hours of their arrival there was kidnapping, rape, and murder. In a 24- to 30-hour period most of the villagers disappeared and were later seen either dead or never seen again. The Prosecutor has proven beyond a reasonable doubt the death of 27 of those victims. The Defence as conceded the death of seven victims: The five members of the Zadro family and Pero and Dragica Maric. These seven deaths by themselves are sufficient to establish the charge of murder, but we have proven many more of those deaths; in fact, all 27 alleged have been proven. An examination of the record indicates that in addition to those seven already conceded by the Defence, witnesses saw three more dead bodies. Witness A testified that he saw Joseph Brekalo by his home. Witness C and Katica Miletic testified that they saw Ilka Miletic lying dead along the roadway. Katica Miletic testified that she saw Ivan Mandic dead along the roadway, somewhat down from Ilka Miletic. With regard to this final deceased, Witness C's sister and brother-in-law were standing not far from Ivan Mandic when he was shot and killed by soldiers. Witness C also helped us to facilitate his secret burial. That's proof of ten of the 27 victims being killed. In addition, refugees living in the area saw nine dead bodies. Zulfo saw Marinko and Luca Maric, Martin Maric, Ilka Maric, Ruza Maric. He even tells the police and the military the location of four of those five deceased. Refugee friends of Witness C saw Mara, Andrija and Dragica Dreznjak and Mara Mandic. Why should we believe these refugees, or why should we indicate that this hearsay testimony is reliable? These refugees came practically starved to Grabovica. It was the villagers who fed them. It was the villagers who helped them. It was the villagers who housed them. And these refugees appreciated that and they reciprocated. They warned some of the villagers of impending danger. They ran off to Jablanica to get police assistance. When they villagers were sent to Jablanica, those that survived, the refugees visited them, brought them clothing, secretly buried a victim, which was Ivan Mandic, and also brought those people news. The refugees had no motive to lie to their new friends. Why lie to the villagers about their friends and relatives? Adnan Solakovic believed them. Ahmed Salihamidzic believed them. And based on the corroboration that we have from other witnesses, this Court can rely on their information too. Soldiers also provided information to the refugees and witnesses about certain deaths. They told of the deaths of Luca Brekalo, Pero and Matija Culjak and Anica Pranjic. Why should we believe them? They had no motive to lie about who was killed. Some of the soldiers had befriended the villagers and provided them information. Their information was also mentioned by others, so corroborated. The statements of soldiers were some sort of, if you want to call it, declaration against the army's interest by analogy should carry an indicia of reliability, just like the evidentiary concept of the declaration against interest. That's 23 of the 27 have been seen dead. Of the final four, the proof of the first two is basic and simple circumstantial evidence. Witness B visits Ljuba and Zivko Dreznjak. ABiH soldiers are outside waiting for a third group of soldiers to arrive. The soldiers are speaking to a Muslim refugee and her daughter. The refugee's name is Munevara Rupeza [phoen]. Witness B leaves the Dreznjaks to escort Munevara and her young daughter back home on the other side of the river. As they walk away, a third group of soldiers arrive. Munevara, who spoke with the soldiers, says, Now they're going to kill them all. Witness B then hears shooting from inside the Dreznjak house, and he hears Ljuba Dreznjak scream. Witness B gets away and hides. The Dreznjaks were never seen alive again. Next time that they are seen is when their family identifies their remains at the hospital in Split with the remains of the other -- or some of the other Grabovica victims. It's obvious what happened to those two poor people. In the words of one of the commanders of the Igman Wolves, they went house to house killing. Finally on the evening of September 8 Ivan Saric and Franjo Ravlic were taken from their home and brought to the bridge. They were taken by soldiers. The soldiers that night weren't taking prisoners; they were taking people out to kill them. A soldier and a refugee told Witness C about it and said that they were likely killed. Ivan was later seen floating in the Neretva but his body was never recovered. Franjo's body was recovered some three months later in a lake; he was buried. This incident was even reported to the security at the hydroelectric plant so they would notify the other -- the police or other civic personnel. They were taken that night -- or on the night they were taken, Witness C -- Witness E testifies that the members of the 9th were taking villagers from their home and killing them. The guard or soldier who spoke to Witness C considered them dead, the police considered them dead, the refugee considered them dead, and they were never seen again. Obviously they were killed. The Prosecutor submits that in addition to those seven bodies or dead bodies that the Defence conceded to, 20 more were proven. The Defence next raises the issue: Who killed those victims in Grabovica. The answer's obvious. The murder was committed by the members of the 9th Motorised Brigade, which was also referred to as Celo's unit or Celo's soldiers. 27 villagers died in approximately 24 to 30 hours. There was no plague in Grabovica, there was no natural disaster. We know that Enes Sakrak received an order from his platoon commander on the morning of September 9th. The order was the villagers were to be killed. By that time Sakrak had already witnessed once if not two murders. Sakrak and two soldiers from his unit, Sead Karic --
