utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, when we left off, Enes Sakrak said that his commander, his platoon leader in the 9th Motorised Brigade gave the order the villagers were to be killed. By that time Sakrak had already witnessed one and possibly two murders. Sakrak and two soldiers went out, they went looking, and they eventually came to the Zadro farm, a small family farm. They found an elderly couple there, a younger couple, and three children. Rajkic and Karagic killed the elderly couple. They then killed the younger man, Mladen Zadro. They took their cow. They took the ring from Ljubica Zadro's finger. Ljubica Zadro was then holding 4-year-old Mladenka. Sakrak shot them, killing mother and child. The soldiers in the 9th Brigade were following their orders. When Sakrak returned he reported to his platoon commander, We killed them. These killings actually began on September 8th. Mustafa Karic of the 2nd Independent Battalion recalls that on the evening of the 8th, "Some of Celo's soldiers came over to us. They said there would be some shooting tonight, so don't pay attention to it." Saban Neziric who was standing guard on the other side of the river stated that the shooting lasted for a considerable period. This was not target practice, this was not a celebration, nor a military operation. It was the murder of Croatian villagers in the village of Grabovica. It was planned and it was based on an order. Witness E tells us what he recalls on that horrible night of September 7th. He tells us on the 7th of March at page 8: "Q. Well, as you stayed in the house, could you hear anything? "A. Yes. "Q. What did you hear during the night? "A. Screaming and shooting which was probably coming from the victims and the soldiers. "Q. What was coming from the victims and the soldiers, sir? "A. Yells. "Q. And how did the other soldiers feel when they heard these yells and screaming? "A. They were confused. It wasn't easy for anyone because we knew what was going on. "Q. What was going on? "A. They were taking the inhabitants away, killing them. "Q. Now, did you have an opinion as to the sobriety of some of those soldiers or -- let me step back, sir. Whose soldiers were taking the inhabitants away and doing this? "A. Celo's soldiers." Witness D also recalls that no one did anything to prevent the killings that night. He identified the murderers as Mustafa Hota and the one who was tried in Sarajevo, which we know to be Enes Sakrak. These were two men from the 9th Brigade. Enes Sakrak, after observing or participating in the murders, spoke with another soldier named Habib Alic, also from the 9th Brigade. Alic told him that he killed a woman in the house after he tried to rape her. Sefko Hodzic spoke with the commander of the Igman Wolves. He was sickened by what he had seen. He was a witness to the murders in Grabovica. He said that they went from house to house killing. They then threw them in the Neretva. The commanders believed that the killers were under the influence the drugs or alcohol. He said: "They even tried to some Bosniak women but some of them were able to escape to our Igman Wolves base." This testimony is consistent with what Witness E tells you, when he says he also saw what he believed to be a rape on the evening of the 8th and it was being committed by Celo's soldiers. Witness C also believed that those members of the 9th Motorised Brigade or Celo's soldiers were under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Vehbija Karic also blamed the 9th Brigade for the crimes committed in Grabovica and believed that drug use was the cause. Ahmed Salihamidzic spoke with Adnan Solakovic in Grabovica Adnan we know is the commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion. He told -- sorry, Solakovic told Salihamidzic that at least five civilians had been killed and Celo's soldiers killed them. Salihamidzic spoke with a soldier who was manning the checkpoint. He told Salihamidzic that the soldiers in the next unit to them were killing the Croat villagers, and he was scared since he was not a Muslim. The soldiers in that next unit were Celo's soldiers. There are many documents which are now exhibits which indicate the soldiers committed the killings, or the soldiers from Sarajevo committed the killings, or Celo's or the 9th Brigade soldiers committed the killings. Namik Djankovic first heard about the killings on September 8th. The talk outside the hotel was that members of the unit from Sarajevo had killed civilians in Grabovica. On September 9th he notified the command in Sarajevo of a killing by BiH soldiers with members of the 9th, and 10th, and 2nd Independent Units in the area. Witness -- I'm sorry, Exhibit 157 is from the commander of the army, Rasim Delic, and it's dated September 12th. And he asked them -- he asked the 6th Corps to check the accuracy of the information regarding the genocide committed against the civilian population by members of the 1st Corps, 9th Brigade. Exhibit 222, Ahmed Salihamidzic wrote that the killings were perpetrated by members of the unit commanded by Ramiz Delalic. Also in that exhibit, that exhibit has two documents, Sajid Brankovic, in his document wrote: "News spread that several Croatian soldiers had been killed and that these murders had been committed by the above-mentioned members of the BH army units from Sarajevo." The above-mentioned units were Celo's units. Exhibit 235 dated September 29th says: The perpetrators have returned to Sarajevo. Also in that document Samir Pezo writes that -- or they write about Samir Pezo that he would not let his Serbian or Croatian soldiers participate in combat for fear that Celo's men would kill them. Returning to Exhibit 222 it says: Celo's soldiers even found out that a member of Zuka's unit was a Croat. They slit his throat, killing him. The evidence has been clear that either Celo's soldiers or members of the 9th Brigade committed the murders. There has been no significant testimony accusing anyone else. The Defence claims that the perpetrators are unknown and Witness C's testimony supports their claim. Witness C said a soldier went to her house and said that he had to kill her because she was a Croat and Ustasha. And she mentioned that he was from these tigers that had been to her house before. The witness, however, says that the tigers came as reinforcements in September and further testifies that they were these new soldiers from Sarajevo. In addition, it should be noted that Witness C's testimony was confusing. She would say one thing, then she would say something different, then she'd start a different answer, then go back to the next answer. But whenever she talked about the tigers and they asked her where the tigers were from, she said, from out north, Sarajevo. In addition to Witness C, one member of the 9th Brigade has admitted to a murder. Another told Enes Sakrak about committing a murder. Three members of the 9th were observed committing murders. Within 24 to 30 hours after the arrival of the 9th Brigade, all of the murders occurred. Members of the 9th were the ones who received those orders to kill and sadly, we submit, obeyed those orders. The Prosecutor submits that it has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the soldiers from the 9th Brigade, or Celo's unit, committed those killings in Grabovica. Now, it is also our argument that these murders occurred because the accused failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent these crimes. I will address the factual basis and Attorney David Re will discuss the legal basis. 27 villagers did not have to die. With basic and proper actions and precautions, these people would have survived. The accused did nothing to prevent the crime in Grabovica from occurring. The Prosecution submits that the accused was more interested in his own glory. He brought the press along on a military operation. He was providing interviews. In Exhibit 289 at page 26, the accused tells Sefko Hodzic, and that is after the Grabovica murders, from the beginning of the war to this point there has not been a greater operation. We suggest that the accused was dreaming of a great command and the glory that would follow and that he lost his focus. And as a result, his actions were reckless. There are no specific and reasonable measures that must be taken to prevent a crime. Rather, a reasonable measure is defined on a case-by-case basis. In this case we will prove that there were none. His failure to prevent these crimes began towards the beginning of the operation and continued through Grabovica. First, the accused failed to select the proper units. His selection of the 9th and 10th Brigades was a colossal error. They had bad reputations. They were undisciplined. They had mistreated the civilians of Sarajevo. Their poor reputation was common knowledge. They may have been good fighters, but they abused civilians. The crimes of the 9th and 10th were common knowledge. There was the theft of property, the theft of vehicles, kidnapping, extortion, drug use, smuggling, beatings, burglary, murder, forced labour, including trench-digging. Everyone in Sarajevo knew about trench-digging. In addition, they started a mutiny in July of 1993. Halilovic knew about these criminal activities. In June of 1993, the accused ordered the formation of a commission to look into trench-digging. Further, high-level meetings were held in Sarajevo where criminal and disciplinary problems of the 9th and 10th Brigades were discussed. The accused was present at those meetings. The Ministry of Interior and the military would meet several times to discuss these criminal activities. Bakir Alispago said that Halilovic's view was that this was a military problem as opposed to a police problem. Ramiz Delalic even says that after the accused attended these meetings he would call us and tell us what was discussed. Basically, the accused knew all about these crime problems, and as we'll shortly know, it was well-known throughout Herzegovina. Halilovic not only selected these units, but he pleaded with Caco to send his 10th Brigade. Sefko Hodzic was at that meeting where Halilovic and Caco spoke. Halilovic believed that Caco was mentally ill. If you look to March 23rd testimony, pages 69 and 70. Hodzic: "Well, when we set out I said, Sefer, that is the first time that I see this Caco person, but I don't think he's all there. And he said, No, he isn't. And he said, Well, I really don't think he is. Well, I couldn't quite say he's a lunatic. I can't remember what sort of word I used then, but I said there was something wrong with him. But he did have good fighters, so he said it is part of reality of war, but he's useful." What we have here is the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina pleading for the assistance of a mad man. When the 6th Corps Chief of Staff Dzevad Tirak learned that those units from Sarajevo had arrived, he was upset and he says because they had a very bad reputation. The corps deputy commander sent Tirak immediately to meet Rasim Delic, the commander of the army, and have those units withdrawn. Here are some just very brief quotes from his testimony of March 30th. Page 65 to 66: "Q. Why did you ask Mr. Delic for the 9th and 10th Brigades to be sent back to Sarajevo? "A. Because I believed that those units were not able to contribute much to any offensive operations. It wasn't only my opinion, it was shared by all members of the 6th Corps command who were there. They could only cause trouble. That's why we asked those units to be withdrawn from the area of responsibility of the 6th Corps as soon as possible. That was why I requested their urgent removal. The news of that -- of this crime that had taken place only reinforced me in this request." That's page 65/66. Another short quote, 54: "Q. What did you tell Delic in respect of that? "A. I must say, I was rather surprised and think I dare say I rather irritated by that and I said, Whoever brought those units to the area did not know what they were doing." Finally on page 47: "Q. You were talking about the track record of the 9th and 10th Brigades in your detailed answer to the Court. Could you explain that? "A. As I said, I can't really say much more. It is my view and not just my view that those two brigades had a reputation for causing trouble and problems." Assuming that you had no option but to take those troops, precautions could -- should have been taken. You don't have to be a military expert to explain the need for cautions. Common sense dictates that. In respect to the soldiers, no limits were placed on the units within the brigades that were being sent. Halilovic could have ordered that no soldiers with criminal records, under investigation, having disciplinary problems, or drug and alcohol problems shall be sent, but he did not. In the Defence brief they state that the assignment of personnel was left to Karavelic. This was another mistake of the accused. Halilovic should have provided selection criteria. He knew about those units. He knew about the problems with those units. He could have acted to protect those people. And there were more failures to prevent the crimes. No order was made to assign or send military police from the 9th Brigade along with those soldiers. There was no order to send the military police to the village of Grabovica, nor was there an order for the 6th Corps military police to be sent to Grabovica. When the soldiers arrived there was no welcome, or so-called welcome, strongly advising them how to act in a village with civilians. There was a failure to properly supervise. Who was in control in Grabovica? We know Zuka or Zulfikar Alispago wasn't there, who they were subordinated to. We know Ramiz Delalic wasn't there. The high-ranking officers visited, but they didn't stay there. No supervision or no strong supervision. Bad troops with criminal tendencies plus no supervision created a dangerous situation. And if you look at the facts, you see it because immediately upon arrival the atmosphere in Grabovica changes. There's shooting, there's shouting. And within hours it turns to murder, rape, and kidnapping. Now, what precautions were taken to protect the villagers? None. Rather the opposite was done. They billeted those problem soldiers with the villagers. These were Croat civilians, civilians from the so-called enemy side, civilians whose relatives they would be fighting against. And what was worse, these were mainly elderly civilians, people who were highly vulnerable. No billeting assessment was performed for these troop accommodation. According to Jusuf Jasarevic, it would have prevented the billeting of troops with civilians. There was no protection of civilians which would have come out of an assessment. The civilians weren't moved out of the area, they were not separated from those troops, there were no guards or police. This was a recipe for disaster. As a result, the trouble began soon and it continued for 24 to 30 hours. The result was 27 dead civilians. Steps should have been taken to prevent those crimes. Witness D sums it up best at page 30 on 21 February. "On the next day when I got up, it was in the morning, 8.00 or 9.00, I'm not sure, and I saw next to the road there were corpses and there was blood. All night this crime had been going on. These murders which no one was able to prevent, or rather nobody paid attention. All these commanders who had been there had nothing to prevent that crime from happening." In summary, the Prosecution submits that the evidence has proven that Sefer Halilovic did not take the necessary and reasonable steps to protect any of those villagers, and as a result they died, 27 died, for nothing. Moving to the villagers of Uzdol. 29 villagers died in Uzdol. The Defence has argued that the Prosecution has failed to establish how they died, who killed them, and that they were civilians. We will address the first two issues together and then the third. The Prosecutor has proven that the villagers did not die as a result of shelling or crossfire. With regard to shelling, a pathologist has testified and provided autopsy reports, statements, and photographs. He concluded that none of those villagers, none of the 27 he examined, two were burned to death, none of those 27 he examined suffered from explosive injuries, rather, they were victim of gunshot wounds, of an axe-like object, or both. We submit that the allegation of shelling was a fraud on this Court. The village was never shelled. Kate Adie from the press, an objective source who came in and visited that village saw no evidence of shelling. Between Kate Adie's video and the video of Kaza Zelenika, there is over one hour of footage. And if you look carefully there are no craters, there are no buildings with holes in the walls, there are no buildings with portions of walls knocked down that you commonly see with shelling. That didn't exist in Grabovica. If the shelling occurred for hours, why no craters? Why? Because as Kazo Zelenika and Kate Adie told you, it never occurred. And if you look at their videos, you can see it never occurred. Why this fraud? Enver Buza needed this fraud to divert blame from the murders of the Prozor Independent Battalion. It was a good try, except the autopsies were performed and the doctor found no explosive wounds. But there's two other little pieces of information that also show that there were no shelling. In this heavy, continuous shelling that these soldiers claim occurred, no HVO soldier was killed. They want you to believe some sort of miracle occurred and that only Croatian property was damaged by the shelling. It is absurd to say that the Croats were shelling strictly their own property. It's unworthy of belief and it's unworthy of belief by this Chamber. The Prosecutor submits that these 29 victims died from intentional acts of murder by ABiH soldiers from the Prozor Independent Battalion. We know that soldiers of the Prozor Independent Battalion attacked Uzdol on orders from the accused. We know that ABiH soldiers were overheard asking, What should we do with the women and children? The answer, Kill all prisoners. We know that Exhibit D315 introduced by the Defence, a book about the deaths in Uzdol, describes what happened. On page 6 of the exhibit, or page 9 of the book it says: "On the 14th of September, 1993, BiH army soldiers invaded Uzdol and began a total massacre. They killed everyone they found there, women, children, old men. They also burned houses, killed cows, oxen, and dogs." What else do we know? That five people, or the murder of five of those 29 were witnessed being killed by ABiH soldiers. Let's step back. Ruza, Marija, and Stjepan Zelic were running from the soldiers who were yelling Allahu Akbar. The were captured. Marko Zelic was hiding in the bushes; he got away. The soldiers called -- the soldiers spoke. They didn't know what happened -- what to do with the women and children. A soldier said to kill all the prisoners and mentioned Enver Buza's name, the commander of the Prozor Independent Battalion. There were then some shots and the soldiers left. Witness came out of the bushes and saw the three dead bodies of his mother, his little brother, and his little sister. Anica Stojanovic was killed outside of her home. Janko Stojanovic, a neighbour, saw it. She was calling for her son, she was falling back. A soldier shot her in the head at close range as she was falling backwards and lands on her back. The pathologist confirmed that the wound to the head was a close-range shot, meaning between five centimetres and one metre, which is just as Janko Stojanovic said. There were four other shots in her body. Janko never explained why she was falling back. It's very possible she was shot then and as she was falling she was shot in the head or someone just shot her after. But what Janko saw was corroborated by medical testimony. These were four executions. The next witness murder is that of Mara Grubisic. She went to the barn. ABiH soldiers set fire to the barn. The flames rose quickly. Witness I saw them set fire to the barn. Her remains were later found and she was buried, or they were buried. In addition to those five witnessed murders, seven were killed at close range during the ABiH attack. Two elderly women were struck with an axe-like weapon. You can see the cutting marks in their skulls. They were Ruza Zelenika and Serafina Stojanovic. Ruza died in her bed and Serafina also died in her home, in her own home. The husbands of both were also killed. Five others were killed at close range by gunshots. Two elderly Croatian women were killed at absolute close range. According to the pathologist, that means the gun was either touching their head or within five centimetres away. Both had head shots. They were Janja Zelenika and Kata Ratkic. In addition, Janja Zelenika was shot at close range. She was lying along a narrow footpath, the wall of a building on one side, shrubbery or bushes on the other, and she was shot at close range. Two elderly men were shot at close range, both right at their doorways, just outside their homes. Those were Mijo Rajic and Martin Ljubic. Also shot at close range behind her home was Kata Ljubic. In his proofing notes that were admitted as an exhibit, Dr. Andjelinovic concluded said that Kata Ljubic was shot at close to five centimetres away. Mato Ljubic was shot at approximately 10 centimetres away, the gun was 10 centimetres away from his body. And Mija Rajic was shot between 20 centimetres and one metre away from his body. The Prosecutor submits that these close-range killings were not the result of crossfire; these were executions. These 12 victims that I've mentioned did not die from crossfire. They did not die from shelling, they were not killed by some sort of accident. They were brutally and intentionally murdered. In addition, seven victims were also killed in their homes under circumstances indicating that they were murdered. Ivka Rajic, that was the woman, if you recall, what had suffered a stroke 13 years earlier. She hadn't been able to walk in years. She was shot three times as she lay in a chair or her bed. Her husband was killed at close range at the doorway. Five neighbours across the street had been killed. We submit that her death was not accidental. Martin Ratkic was killed, you might remember that one. He was the one who was embracing with his wife and they were both dead. They were lying right next to each other. He had an ear that was severed while he was alive. There was a lot of cross-examination on that issue, but on re-examination the doctor produced one of his own photographs, and it depicts this cutting edge or cutting line on the ear, which he said based on that he was able to determine that that ear was severed while he was alive. As a result, Martin Ratkic was attacked at close range and his death must be deemed intentional. Jadranka and Ivan Zelenika were killed in their home. Jadranka was the little girl, Ivan was the older man, her grandfather. Her grandmother Ruza, you might recall, was lying in the bed. Her head had been blown off. Actually, she was the one who had the axe-type cutting to the head and there was also possible shots to the head. She also had four shots to the body. Little Jadranka was also dead in that house. Earlier in that morning their barn was set on fire. Marko Zelic goes by and he sees the barn on fire and he sees Ivan outside his house with a soldier. Moments later or minutes later there is an order to kill, and Marko Zelic hears the shooting and sees the death of three of his -- three members of his family. Right around the corner from that, the Zelenika house is here -- we don't have use of the computer. The Zelenika house is right here, the Zelic house is here, and right next to it, diagonally across from the Zelenika house, are those three dead bodies. These deaths, we submit, were not accidental or the result of crossfire. Two elderly women, Luca Zelenika and Kata Perkovic, were both killed in their homes. Their homes do not appear to be looted or disturbed. These people were living in Zelenika in a cluster of homes. If you look at Exhibit 300, everyone in that cluster of homes, a woman in all of those homes had been killed, which is consistent with Kate Adie's testimony of a systematic, house-to-house killing, which is also corroborated by Marko Zelic's testimony, kill all prisoners, which is also corroborated by Exhibit 315 introduced by the Defence, noting that BiH soldiers killed everyone they found, which is also corroborated by Ivka Stojanovic's testimony where soldiers said she was dead as she lay there motionless. And they went looking for another. When they went looking for another, they weren't looking for prisoners to bring back to Hari [phoen]. We submit they were looking for people to kill. Finally we see the both of -- I'm sorry, the death of Jela Dzalto who died in a fire in the Prskalo house. Exhibit 315 explains that she went into the house and wouldn't come out, so the BiH soldiers set it on fire. We submit that's an execution. That's not a killing by crossfire or accident. Ten villagers were killed outside of their homes in circumstances consistent with murder. Two elderly men were killed outside of their home -- of their homes. 87-year-old Franjo Stojanovic was shot, and here's the quote: "While his body was at a relative rest." "Body was a relative rest." Anto Stojanovic was shot four times. In the three closest homes to him, the victims were killed at close range, and you can see those homes in Exhibit 302, and the victims are Kata Ratkic, Anica Stojanovic and Serafina Stojanovic. These old men were lying outside their homes without any shoes. Their deaths and those of their neighbours are consistent with a house-to-house execution. Dragica Zelenika was shot and her body was partially burned. She also died in that cluster of homes in Zelenika. If we look at -- if we can get Exhibit 301 -- or 300 on the screen. I heard it's working. If we look at -- 301 will be fine. If we look at 301, we see the markings, 4, 5, 6, 7. It's directly in the centre to the left. It's a -- you'll see it soon, but it's a cluster of homes. And what's interesting -- I'm not sure if the system's working. The women in those homes were killed in each of those homes. Now, where Dragica Zelenika was killed, Witness I sees soldiers fighting. We don't have it. I'll just continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we saw it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Oh, thank you. Now, Witness I tells you in that area she was shot at, a barn was set on fire, she could hear soldiers yelling Allahu Akbar. The soldiers said they were going to come back for her. It's our contention that Dragica, like the others, died intentionally. She was murdered. Finally, there are seven villagers who were killed just outside their homes -- outside two homes. In one we have Domin Rajic, Ivka Rajic, and Zorka Glibo and they are with their son, Ivan Rajic. And in the other we have Lucija Rajic, Sima Rajic, Stanko Rajic and Mara Rajic. In our brief we argued that based on the position and locations of those bodies and their wounds it appeared that these victims were lined up and executed or that they were ambushed, and that's at paragraphs 405 to 409 and 417 to 420 in our brief. If you look at the three bodies in a row of Lucija Rajic, Sima Rajic and Stanko Rajic in Exhibit 312 at 4839 to 4848, you see them lined up in a row. You see that it looks -- something looks wrong, like they were lined up and killed. Let's go back to Exhibit 315. What does it say with regard to Stanko and Lucija Rajic? It says Stanko and Lucija Rajic were captured and placed in front of the Prskalo house with Sima and Mara Rajic and killed. That's page 42 of the book and that's concerning the information of Lucija Rajic. And what does it say about Domin and Ivka Rajic? It says that they were also killed after their son was executed. Not only were these 29 deaths murders, they were committed by the ABiH soldiers. Those soldiers from the Prozor Independent Battalion, they were the ones that were present. They had the motive to kill. They had failed in their mission. Some had served as human shields by the Croats and they had been displaced from Prozor. They had received orders to kill. According to Ivka Stojanovic, they were searching for others to kill. Five of their killings, if not six were witnessed. They were burning buildings and destroying civilian property, and then they lied about the shelling to try and cover their acts. It's obvious who committed those acts, the members of the ABiH from the Prozor Independent Battalion. Finally, the Prosecution submits that these victims were civilians. None of these victims were dressed in uniform. Several of them didn't even have shoes. Not one was identified as firing at soldiers. Not one was identified as carrying a firearm on that day. Most were dressed in traditional village clothing. Three of the victims were young children. The Defence claim that two women who baked bread for the soldiers were not civilians; they are Kata Ljubic and Mara Rajic. The women who helped out in the kitchen did not wear uniforms, they did not carry weapons. Those people who volunteered to bake, to cook, to clean, or distribute food were not involved in hostilities. These victims were not at the school when they were killed nor were they with soldiers. They died with their families. Domin Rajic was killed outside of his home. There's no evidence that he was involved in combat at the time. He wasn't at the school. He died with his family. He died near his son, who was wearing a uniform, and you can see the difference. Domin and his wife dressed as basic villagers and his son in a uniform. According to Exhibit 315, he and his wife were executed after their son, a soldier, was executed. The documents that the Defence produces, indicating that Kata Ljubic and Domin Rajic died, that they died while carrying out orders. We know, according to the testimony of Kazo Zelenika that that wasn't true. They weren't on the front lines. When they asked Kazo Zelenika about Kata Ljubic being on the front line, he thought it was ridiculous. They weren't at the school. Kazo, who was the registrar for the area, he knew the people, he was part of the local unit, he didn't even believe that Domin Rajic had been mobilised, nor was Kata baking for the soldiers at that time. He said that Kata was baking for the soldiers when the war started and that was it. The Prosecution submits that these documents which entitled family to benefits were a gift. They were a gift that were given to families. They weren't based on what had occurred, and they do not convert these people into being soldiers. Ruza Zelenika allegedly threw a hand-grenade, not to wage war but as a diversion so she and her children could escape. So even if you believe the testimony that she threw a hand-grenade -- or the book that says she threw a hand-grenade, was she fighting with the soldiers? Did she stay and shoot at them with guns? No. She threw a hand-grenade out one window and they got out of the house. And what did they do? Did they go out and fight? No. They ran for their lives. Should a single act of self-defence convert her civilian status into that of being involved hostilities? We suggest that it should not. These people ran off, they were captured, they were held. A determination had to be made what to do with the women and children, and sadly there was an order to kill all prisoners. Now, the Defence alleges that the villagers suddenly rose up and took the defence of the village. Where's the proof? Who did this? The elderly? The infirm? The little children? All they have is a report from Enver Buza which says that his troops were fighting armed civilians. Whose got the motive to lie? Buza sure has. His soldiers are allegedly involved in a war crime. His report about the incident, according to the chief of security, Nermin Eminovic, the chief of security from the 6th Corps, was viewed as not serious. Mr. Eminovic said it has false figures as to the numbers killed -- or actually, we claim it had false figures as to the numbers that were killed. He's talking about 65 people killed. We know from the death certificates that 65 weren't killed. Eminovic says the numbers were as if they were being given off the top of one's head. The head of security didn't take the report seriously. We claim that the report is not reliable and suggest nor should the Court. Who rose up and fought against the ABiH? There's no testimony of anyone grabbing a gun and fighting. The fact that there might have been guns in their homes, they were farmers and hunters in the area, the fact that soldiers occasionally stayed in their homes does not convert those civilians into being soldiers nor does it make them legitimate targets. Finally, the Defence claims in paragraph 57: "There is no evidence of any of the unidentified perpetrators in Uzdol -- perpetrator in Uzdol was aware at that time that any persons which he might have killed was a civilian, and with that knowledge he intentionally and deliberately killed him." I'd like to show the Court some video clips and let the Court determine whether or not someone looking at these people would believe that they were civilians. We're going to be using Sanction. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Stjepan Zelic, the little boy who's not wearing pants, no stockings or no shoes. Does this look like a soldier taking part in hostilities? Could we go to next one, please. Could we go to Jadranka Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is Marija Zelic, a 13- or 14-year-old girl. Do we see any guns? Do we see any shell casings near her? She doesn't even have shoes. Would anyone believe that she was taking part in hostilities? Could we go to Jadranka Zelenika, 35.22. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We see Jadranka Zelenika here with her grandmother. Is there anyone who's going to say that that little child was a soldier taking part in hostilities or her grandmother who's next to her with a head that was partially chopped off? Since we're having trouble with the system, you can look at the others. Look at Luca Rajic, Sima Rajic, Ivka Rajic, the paralysed woman killed in her bed. Look at the others. Kata Petkovic, the elderly lady, if you remember, lying in her own home with the thick glasses. Any soldier seeing these people would have known that these are civilians, and if there was any question, the benefit goes to them as being civilians. The Prosecutor submits that any soldier who wanted to distinguish would have been able to determine that these were civilians and not soldiers. But the soldiers of the Prozor Independent Battalion weren't trying to distinguish who was a civilian; all they were trying to do was kill. The Prosecutor submits that we have proven beyond a reasonable doubt that 29 civilians were killed in the village of Uzdol on that date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. And I think that we should have a break and we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll continue until 1.45, then we stop. And in the afternoon this courtroom will be used for a judgement hearing by the Appeals Chamber. Then we'll resume at 3.45. I understand that the Prosecution has not used up the time allocated to them. Mr. Re, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Indeed, I am. Thank you, Your Honours. I will be speaking about several issues. I will address in slightly more detail how the Prosecution has proved that Mr. Halilovic was in command and control and had effective control over the soldiers that committed the two massacres. I will also expand upon some things Mr. Weiner referred to under the heading of failure to prevent. I will address a number of Defence arguments. To let the Trial Chamber know where I'm going, the Defence legal arguments that I will specifically address are under the following headings: The pleadings, the particulars, the armed conflict, the nexus, the body of law, the legal issue of levee en masse, causality and failure to punish, acquiescence, the pre-existing legal duty, the state of law, whether Mr. Halilovic acted in accordance with Bosnian law. I will also address the two issues of failure to punish in both of the crime base areas of Uzdol and Grabovica. The first area I wish to address is that of command and control and how the Prosecution has proved that Mr. Halilovic was in command and control of the units that perpetrated the massacres in Grabovica and Uzdol. I'll move to several specific examples. Now, at the end of the case it is, the Prosecution submits, apparent that the evidence is both direct and circumstantial as to his method of control. One of the ways which we have shown that he had command and control is through direct evidence relating to the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades and the 2nd Independent Battalion travelling to Grabovica in September 1993. The Prosecution has produced -- adduced direct evidence of the subordination and of the orders to and from Mr. Halilovic, to which the only conclusion which can be drawn is that he was in command of both the operation and of all the units that participated in Operation Neretva. Now, General Vahid Karavelic was crucial to the Prosecution's case in this respect. His evidence was that he, that's General Karavelic, who, in the Prosecution's submission, was a very impressive person and a very impressive if not charismatic witness with absolutely no axe to grind, no hidden agenda, and came here as a witness of truth to assist the Trial Chamber in its quest for the truth. Mr. Karavelic, who was in the very, very difficult position of being in charge of the Defence of Sarajevo from the encircled Bosnian Serb forces attended the Zenica meeting in August 1993. Now, he says at the end -- his evidence was at the end of August or early September, Mr. Halilovic ordered him to send units to Herzegovina for operations in the Neretva Valley. Mr. Karavelic resisted this. He was afraid of taking soldiers from the Defence of Sarajevo. Now, the Trial Chamber has to ask itself: Why is Mr. Halilovic ordering Mr. Karavelic to send soldiers anywhere if Mr. Halilovic did not have the power to do so? The Trial Chamber has heard extensive evidence which is not opposed by -- which is common to both sides, that the Chief of Staff has no -- of an army has no command functions except those delegated to him by the commander. Now, why would Mr. Halilovic, if he was not indeed in charge of the Operation Neretva, the operation to clear the blockade of Mostar, be sending orders to corps commanders, generals, to take troops from desperately needed on the outskirts of Sarajevo to another operation? Now, Karavelic's response was to resist this, but Mr. Halilovic then sent Mr. Karavelic a written order; that's Exhibit P161. Mr. Karavelic was of the view that it was illogical. That was the order in which Mr. Halilovic asked for specific units. Mr. Karavelic's reaction to that was, Well, it was logical to ask for the Delta Brigade, it was logical to ask for the 2nd Independent Battalion because they were mobile units, but it was not logical, in military terms, to ask for parts of the 9th or 10th Brigades. Now, that's of course something Your Honours can use, the Trial Chamber can use, in assessing Mr. Halilovic's mens rea. Mr. Weiner touched upon the criminal activities, the known criminal activities, of the 9th and 10th Brigades in Sarajevo. And the fact that Mr. Halilovic knowing of their criminal propensities and indeed actions was prepared to personally select these two brigades goes to his mens rea of his failure to prevent what later occurred in Grabovica. Now, what was Karavelic's reaction to receiving this order from Mr. Halilovic? Well, Mr. Karavelic, because of his concern, contacted the commander, General Rasim Delic. It was only after Delic told Karavelic that he, Karavelic, should act in accordance with Halilovic's orders that Karavelic was prepared to accede to them. Mr. Karavelic gave the reason of why he contacted Mr. Delic was because it was a basic military rule that the commander is a superior to a Chief of Staff. Now, on the 2nd of September, and that's Exhibit P382, Mr. Halilovic carried through by asking -- by writing to Mr. Karavelic again asking for an urgent response to his earlier request for the troops to be sent to Neretva. In response to Halilovic's orders, what did Karavelic do? Well, he responded in accordance what Delic told him he should do, and that is to send the troops. So he issued orders to the troops to go there. For example, Exhibit P83 is the order of the 4th of September, 1993, to Ramiz Delalic, Celo, in person ordering him to send troops, soldiers, to Bradina, that is two platoons of 25 men each to launch an offensive. Karavelic said that he also issued similar orders to the 2nd Independent Battalion, the 10th Brigade and the Delta Brigade. Karavelic followed this up by writing to Mr. Halilovic by telling him, that's Exhibit P384, that the soldiers were on their way. Now, as we -- as you heard the soldiers didn't go that day because of inclement weather. And Mr. Karavelic on the 6th of the September wrote to Mr. Karavelic, that's Exhibit -- I'm sorry, Mr. Halilovic on Exhibit P290, explaining the delay. The same day in Exhibit P385 he issued an order to the commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion about travelling to Jablanica, telling them that combat activities in the area were to be carried out under the command of a group from the supreme command. Well, who was commanding that group? It was Sefer Halilovic. That's Mr. Karavelic's testimony at page 44 to 49 on the 20th of April, 2005. Under military doctrine and under the evidence and on the evidence in this case the situation was that after the troops -- that Mr. Karavelic had command and control of these particular troops, that's the soldiers from the 9th and the 10th, from the time they left his subordination of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo until the time that they reached the supreme command group headed by Mr. Halilovic in Jablanica. Now, the point of handover could have been, according to Mr. Karavelic, Sarajevo or Jablanica. But the Prosecution's submission is that once they left his command their subordination was transferred to Mr. Halilovic's, whether it be from the point they left in Sarajevo or the point they arrived in Jablanica does not really matter. The point of the subordination is they were being transferred from the command of one general to the command of another, that was they were being transferred from Mr. Karavelic's command directly to Mr. Halilovic's command. And it is indeed a normal principle of command and control in an army that troops must be under the subordination of someone. And in fact, Mr. Halilovic's order of the 6th of September, that is Exhibit P122, makes it quite clear that he had control of those troops because he resubordinated them to Zulfikar Alispago, that's Zuka. That clearly sets out the delineation of command and control. The subordination was clear. It was the 9th and the 10th and the 2nd, went from Sarajevo to Mr. Halilovic, and Mr. Halilovic did what any commander does, and that is he resubordinated them to the appropriate unit on the ground. And not for one moment did Mr. Halilovic lose his command and control over those units because Zuka was subordinated to his inspection team -- Zuka's unit was subordinated to him, and through Zuka the 9th and 10th Brigades were subordinated to Mr. Halilovic. There are other orders in that same period which in the Prosecution's submission graphically demonstrate that Mr. Halilovic was exercising command and control over all the units in the Grabovica area. There was of course the order Karavelic sent on the 6th of September, which is P385, referring to an agreement with Halilovic or Delic in relation to carrying out offensive combat operations for the purposes of liberating the Jablanica-Mostar communication. He said combat activities in that area are to be carried out under the control of a group from the supreme command staff led by the Chief of Staff, that's Mr. Halilovic. And in that he referred to the agreement of seven days. That was the period in which those soldiers were going to be under Mr. Halilovic's control or command. Now, why would Mr. Karavelic be referring to combat activities being carried out under the control of a group led by Mr. Halilovic if in fact that were not happening? Why would the general in charge of all those troops in Sarajevo all subordinated to him be sending them to Mostar -- the Mostar area if they were not in fact subordinate -- to be subordinated to Mr. Halilovic? A crucial aspect of Mr. Karavelic's evidence in relation to command and control was he testified that Adnan Solakovic, the commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion, had contacted Mr. Karavelic when he was there, requesting that the soldiers be allowed to return. It was a coded message, and the details are in Exhibit P72, that's the 11th of September, and they spoke for about a minute or so. What is in P72 is consistent with the conversation as relayed by Mr. Karavelic to this Court. Now, the crucial part is that Karavelic testified that he could not have ordered the return of Mr. Solakovic without Mr. Halilovic's permission, otherwise it would have been a gross breach of discipline. That's another factor indicating that Mr. Halilovic commanded the units in Grabovica. In addition, there's the order to attack, Exhibit D273, of the 11th of September, 1993. It's a binding combat order and it could only have been derived from the document resubordinating all the units of the 1st Corps to Zuka's troops. In fact, Mr. Karavelic testified that Mr. Solakovic's unit was subordinated to Zuka's unit by Mr. Halilovic's order. We ask the Trial Chamber to pay particular attention to that evidence which is at page 78 on the transcript of the 20th of April this year. It also -- there's Exhibit P388, which is a request from Mr. Karavelic to Mr. Halilovic at the IKM in Jablanica asking him to respect the orders, respect the agreement, and return those parts of the 2nd Independent Battalion, the 9th and the 10th on the 12th and 13th of September, 1993. He testified that he needed the 2nd back because it was a mobile in a reserve unit. Now, all those things which I've just referred to, in our submission, go directly to the fact that Mr. Halilovic was exercising command and control by issuing orders to very, very senior officers such as Mr. Karavelic, and those orders were in fact obeyed. Another factor which points to Mr. Karavelic -- or Mr. Halilovic's control is that of the existence of the forward command post, which is referred to by its initials "IKM." Now, an IKM in general terms is a centre from which a commander can issue commands while a commander is in the field. On the 1st of September, Mr. Halilovic and his inspection team established one, an IKM, at the Jablanica hydroelectricity power station. It is abundantly obvious from the evidence that everyone from -- the most senior officers in the Bosnian army, corps commanders, Mr. Gusic, Mr. Karavelic believed that Mr. Halilovic was operating a forward command post from that point and was coordinating and commanding combat operations from -- from the IKM in Jablanica. Mr. Gusic, the 4th Corps commander who, in the Prosecution's submission, had absolutely no reason not to be telling the truth on this, and his evidence is of course amply corroborated by all the documents flowing forwards and backwards from the IKM with IKM written on them. He testified that Mr. Halilovic was in fact the commander at the IKM and in that capacity issued binding orders to other commanders and they would carry out all orders given by the IKM under the command of Sever Halilovic. That testimony is at page 63 and 64 on the 3rd of February this year. And most significantly, Mr. Gusic testified that he as the 4th Corps commander, again, like Karavelic, only subordinate to Halilovic if he's in the -- in a line of command and control, a chain of command, testified that he, Gusic, would not refuse to obey Halilovic's orders. As you've heard the evidence, if Halilovic is merely the Chief of Staff he is not in a position to issue binding orders unless directed to or authorised to do by the commander. Now, Gusic who would know, who was there on the spot, also testified that the Operation Neretva was coordinated and carried out from that forward command post and that Halilovic was in charge of that operation. Now, Mr. Halilovic himself of course in his own report, that's Exhibit P130 of the inspection team, himself acknowledges the existence of the IKM. And he said, An IKM was set up in Jablanica where the team planned the operation which covered the wide front from Gornji Vakuf and Mostar and the valleys of Neretva and Vrba rivers and ensured logistic means for the operation. Now, when the soldiers went back to Sarajevo in September and Halilovic was requesting from Karavelic their return, where did Karavelic send his response to? Karavelic ordered Delalic on the 24th of September, 1993, and that's Exhibit P395, he ordered Delalic to send 125 men to Vrdi Jablanica and to report to the commander of the IKM. Again, another crucial piece of evidence as to the role of the IKM and the role of Sefer Halilovic. In our final trial brief we pointed out in pages 73 to 74 a number of factors which we say the Prosecution has proved are all consistent with Mr. Halilovic issuing and -- issuing orders and having them obeyed, which of course is one of the indicia of effective control. And rather than go through them, I invite the Trial Chambers, in due course, you will examine them in some detail. The next issue is that of failure to prevent, and I pick up from where Mr. Weiner left off. The test for failure to prevent is that a commander must take all reasonable and necessary measures within his material abilities to prevent the offence or punish the offender. Now, what the case law establishes, and this is quite important, is that this must be decided on a case-by-case basis and there is no rigid definition of what all this means. The Defence in their final trial brief have made complaint that the Prosecution has failed to particularise within the indictment all the reasonable and necessary measures that a commander could take. The Prosecution's response to this is the following: The Prosecution does not need to particularise each and everything that a commander should or should not have done in the indictment. The Prosecution in this case has given the Defence all the notice they need of what we say our case was. It's in the indictment, it's in the pre-trial brief, it was in the opening, and it was in the evidence. Our pre-trial -- our final trial brief has listed the following matters which we say Mr. Halilovic should have done and omitted to do and thereby failed to prevent -- and failed in his duties as a commander. And they are: He failed to exercise care in the selection of units. By bringing the very same units from Sarajevo who were known -- with their known criminal propensities, who were carrying out acts -- crimes against the civilian population, the robbery, the extortion, and most seriously the trench-digging, kidnapping civilians off the streets and taking them to the front lines where they're exposed to enemy fire and exposed to possible death, which the Defence in its final trial brief dismisses as a misdemeanour. The members of the Trial Chamber know better than it is a misdemeanour. It would be a grave offence in any civilised society, not less within a war. By taking those very same soldiers, by choosing those soldiers, Mr. Halilovic failed in his ability to prevent the crimes in Grabovica. Upon the arrival of those troops in Grabovica, Mr. Halilovic failed to issue warnings to them. He knew who these people were. He knew that elements within the 9th and the 10th were committing these grave crimes in Sarajevo against a civilian population, yet he failed to so much as send anyone down there to issue a warning, to speak to them. The only evidence before the Trial Chamber of contact between the inspection team or members of the supreme command and the soldiers on the ground is to talk to them about -- to talk to them about accommodation, not to warn them in the strongest possible terms that they are here amongst civilians and you must respect the lives of these civilian people. You must respect their health. You must not harm them in anyway. Nothing like that happened. Another failure by Mr. Halilovic was the failure to perform a security assessment or an analysis for the billeting of the soldiers. Now, that's very basic, in the Prosecution's submission. If you were going to billet or accommodate soldiers amongst civilians - and it's compounded here by these being soldiers of one army or ethnicity, a controlling army - amongst the occupied citizens of another ethnicity, the most basic thing you would do would be to perform a security assessment of what is happening in that village and how you could protect those civilians from what might occur. Now, even Mr. Jasarevic, the chief of military administration, said in his evidence, and I highlight this, the fact that it wasn't controlled -- it wasn't performed, he said, and that's on page 87 on the 1st of March. He said: "It is precisely one of the key mistakes that this assessment wasn't carried out. And I don't know why it wasn't carried out because when one estimates the strength of one's own forces and the terrain, our security would never propose that a unit or the unit of... Celo, be billeted in the region, in the waiting area, which would be a location to the rear of combat area, to some Croat village, when they are about to embark upon -- into with Croats, some of whom are from that village." The Prosecution's submission is Mr. Halilovic failed utterly in his duty in relation to performing the most basic measure to prevent harm to those villagers. And from that comes the failure to recognise, the basic failure to recognise the danger of billeting those very troops with those particular villagers. Mr. Jasarevic in evidence - and we're not just saying this with hindsight - he recognised it. He said in evidence at pages 13 and 14 on the 18th -- sorry, 87 on the 1st of March. "It was stupid to billet the men in a village inhabited by Croats. The inhabitants were all Croats in the village. There were no Bosniaks. And in the immediate vicinity of that village was a defence line manned by Croat soldiers." Now, the dangers of doing this manifested themselves that very afternoon that the 9th and 10th Brigades arrived from Sarajevo when members of the 9th and 10th brigades shot dead innocent Croat villagers in the homes in which they were billeted. Now, apart from that, apart from the basic failures, before -- before accommodating them, Mr. Halilovic failed to have his staff, those under his command, plan or prepare for the security of the villagers when the 9th Brigade was there. The failures there range from the most basic preparation, that is not using military police, to the more complex, such as moving villagers out or closing off a section of the village, that is billeting the -- or accommodating the soldiers away from the Croats, the Bosnian Croats. Nothing like that happened. They were basically told to go find accommodation for yourself with the enemy. Now, once they were there, there was no proper supervision of the soldiers, elements of whom came from the notorious 9th Brigade. And in this we ask you to take into account the evidence of Mr. Arnautovic and Kapur. Mr. Arnautovic of course was someone who was sent by Celo with the soldiers to the 9th, and he was one of the people who was rounded up in operation Trebevic. He was one of the people who was held, imprisoned, and interrogated; he says mistreated. The people who were imprisoned, who were detained after Trebevic were the worst. Some of the worst were in Grabovica in September 1993. Notwithstanding that, there was absolutely no supervision of the soldiers when they were there. Now, Mr. Halilovic also failed to provide written orders to the soldiers. His failure in that respect is graphically demonstrated by Exhibit -- an order to attack drafted by Witness Behlo, a Defence witness, for Enver Zeljagic on the 15th of September, 1993 in which Mr. Behlo found it was necessary to include in an order: "I most strictly prohibit looting, slaughtering, and killing of innocent civilians while prisoners of war shall be treated according to the regulations on prisoners of war." Now, why did, Your Honours, Mr. Behlo feel it necessary to include this specific clause in his orders? His testimony on this point was quite telling. It was because he wished to prevent or to take some measures, reasonable and necessary measures, to prevent any harm occurring to civilians during a military operation. Mr. Behlo, an ABiH soldier, said this type of clause was needed when soldiers would be fighting in "inhabited areas." His testimony on that point is at page 41 and 42 on the 28th of June this year. Now, of course Mr. Behlo, and the Prosecution assumes the Trial Chamber has seen similar orders because we certainly have in the course of our work here, Mr. Behlo said he had seen that type of order or that sort of clause before, but no where will you see that clause in the orders before the Court that Mr. Halilovic issued, and Mr. Halilovic issued no orders through his subordinates in writing directed to the soldiers of the 9th and 10th Brigades he brought from Sarajevo not to harm or kill civilians and to respect conventions relating to civilians and prisoners of war. The final issue we have highlighted under failure to prevent is that in relation to the remarks of Mr. Karic. Now, the Prosecution puts its case on Mr. Karic's remarks as follows. There is evidence before the Trial Chamber that Mr. Karic made inappropriate, if indeed, reprehensible remarks in relation to accommodating the -- accommodating the soldiers amongst the Croats. The Prosecution is well aware that Mr. Karic disputes making those remarks and that the evidence is divided upon. This having heard the evidence, the Prosecution would be entitled to make a positive finding that he indeed did make those remarks. Now, if the Prosecution -- if the Trial Chamber makes that finding and also makes the finding, because there is some evidence that Mr. Halilovic was present and heard them, the Trial Chamber should find that Mr. Halilovic failed in his duty by failing to react appropriately and in the strongest possible terms when Mr. Karic made his remarks about throwing the civilians into the river. If that happened -- if the Trial Chamber is satisfied that happened and it happened when it happened and Mr. Halilovic was there, the only finding the Trial Chamber can make is that it is a gross failure by Mr. Halilovic to react, condemn Mr. Karic on the spot, discipline him, and make it quite clear to the assembled troops that this was not to be countenanced and to immediately issue a countermanding order. The Prosecution being aware of the division of evidence on this particular respect submits that the Prosecution case does not rely in any way, whether or not it's pleaded in the indictment, on this particular failure. The failures by Mr. Halilovic in every other respect are so manifest that the Prosecution, in our respectful submission, has proven its case beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Halilovic did nothing, let alone take any reasonable or necessary measures, to prevent the crimes in Grabovica. We're saying the Trial Chamber can make a finding that the Karic gesture didn't occur or make no finding on it or make no finding as to whether or not Mr. Halilovic was there and still be well and truly satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of all the other failures that we have identified. And in this respect it's important to note the case law, that there is no rigid definition of what constitutes reasonable and necessary measures. It has to be decided on a case-by-case basis. And the things I've just outlined to the Trial Chamber are those which would be necessary on a case-by-case basis according to the circumstances in Grabovica: Troops of known criminal propensity being billeted or accommodated amongst civilians and civilians of a different ethnicity. Those are the particular circumstances pertaining to this particular case. And when we've submitted before that the case law has been on the ground as to what exactly a commander should do, I challenge anyone to find a case which is on -- precisely on point here. In which a court in the world has set out those particular measures. These measures are all those which we say would have been necessary in the circumstances, and they're not just obvious now but should have been and were obvious very much so at the time. The Defence has claimed at some length in its final trial brief that the Prosecution's pleadings are inadequate and the indictment is in some way defective. Now, the Prosecution responds, and if I could put up document 5 which is the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision through Sanction. The Prosecution responds that we have met all the pleading requirements identified by the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision at paragraph 218 of the judgement. Your Honours can see before you the decision of the Appeals Chamber, and I will just briefly go through paragraph 218 -- 218(a) and (b). We must identify, (1), the accused is a superior. Well, we did that in the indictment, the pre-trial brief and the opening. (2), subordinate sufficiently identified. Yes, we did that. It was the 9th, the 10th, the 4th, the Prozor Independent Battalion. We've identified the -- sorry, number (3): Over whom he had effective control. Well, we've identified those as well. That's the 9th Brigade which committed the crimes in Grabovica and the Prozor Independent Battalion which committed the crimes in Uzdol. (4), and for whose acts he is alleged to be responsible. Same again. Turning to (B): "The conduct of the accused by which he may be found to have known or had reason to know the crimes were about to be committed. Again, the Prosecution has done that in the indictment, pre-trial brief, opening, and by the evidence in the documents we provided to the Defence. And (ii),"the related conduct of others for whom he is alleged to be responsible." Again, we have done this. Turning to 219. With respect to the mens rea there are two ways in which the relevant state of mind may be pleaded. "(i), either the specific state of mind itself should be pleaded as a material fact; or (ii), the evidentiary facts from which a statement of mind is to be inferred should it be pleaded. Each of the material facts must be -- must usually be pleaded expressly, although in some circumstances it may suffice if they are expressed by necessary implication." We have done that. In each and every case we have identified the units the form of control the accused was exercising, who he was exercising it, the units who were subordinated to him. We've identified their conduct, what they did, who they were. We've identified the fact that the accused was on notice, how he found out, and what he did or didn't do. So in our respectful submission, we have completely complied with everything set out in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision. Another aspect of the pleadings, and I briefly touched upon this earlier, very, very earlier, in the response to the Defence notice filed on Friday is that the Defence is making very, very late complaint of these issues. The Prosecution's submission is that these matters, those of pleadings, particulars, are now res judicata between the parties. There are four particular decisions in which the Trial Chamber and the pre-trial Chamber, or five actually, have issued decisions which are binding on the parties for the purposes of the trial. These were the one of the 1st of April, 2003, the Defence motion pursuant to 65 ter (K) requesting the Pre-Trial Judge to grant relief from waiver and to grant relief pursuant to Rule 72. Well, what that basically was was a request to re-open the proceedings and re-open the challenge to the indictment, which should have been made within 30 days of the indictment being filed and doing it some 18 months later. The Pre-Trial Chamber ruled that they couldn't do it. The 11th of July, 2003, there was a decision on the Defence complaint on the Pre-Trial Chamber direction, which was a repetition where the Pre-Trial Chamber repeated its order after another motion was filed. There was also the decision of the Pre-Trial Chamber on the 16th of December, 2003, on the Defence motion for particulars, and that decision the Pre-Trial Chamber refused to certify in January -- for appeal in January 2004. The issue, the Prosecution submits, is closed for the trial. If there's an appeal point, the Defence are perfectly entitled to take it, but they can't take it now. The Pre-Trial Chamber has ruled -- the Trial Chamber has ruled that they have been adequately provided with particulars. The indictment is not vague and that they have everything they needed to defend the case against them. To which, or course, the question is always to be raised: What is, or what was the prejudice to the accused? What possible prejudice could have accrued by the combination of the Prosecution pleading its case, as the law entitles it to in the pre-trial brief, the indictment, the service of statements and documents, and the opening statement. There's no prejudice. They have been fully informed and on notice of our case with adequate time to prepare and adequate time to make any proper challenge that they wish to make. In this respect, I wish to refer the Trial Chamber to the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory decision -- I'm sorry. The decision of the 11th of March, 2005, in Hadzihasanovic; that's document 10 of the Appeals Chamber. The decision on joint defence -- interlocutory appeal of Trial Chamber decision on Rule 98 bis motions for acquittal. And I refer the Trial Chamber to paragraph 10 of that decision on page 5. And if you look at the second sentence -- if you look at the first and second sentences, if you go down to the second sentence where the Trial Chamber -- where the Appeals Chamber says: "Given that it was clear at that time, the Prosecution was not expressly pleading the nature of the armed conflict, and that the Prosecution was proceeding on the basis that Article 3 applied to both international and non-international conflicts, it might be inferred that the appellants saw a tactical advantage in waiting until this time to appeal." Now, the Prosecution submits that exactly the same considerations apply and the Trial Chamber should treat all of the submissions in the final trial brief of the Defence as to pleadings, particulars and the form of the indictment. They've been raised and dismissed before and now they've waited right until the end and are again trying to use it for their own tactical advantage, which brings me to the issue of the failure to plead the armed conflict of which the Defence has complained at page 1 of its brief. Now, Ms. Chana has dealt with this in some -- has passed -- has dealt with this in passing in relation to the type of conflict which must be pleaded. The law is so crystal clear in relation to pleading of an armed conflict that the Prosecution does not understand why this has been raised again. I again refer to the Hadzihasanovic decision, but this time the Hadzihasanovic decision on -- the interlocutory decision on the challenge to jurisdiction of the 16th of July, 2003. And I refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 28 and 29 of that decision. If you look at the last line of paragraph 28 in relation to additional protocols I and II. And then paragraph 29: "The Appeals Chamber affirms the view of the Trial Chamber that command responsibility was part of customary international law relating to international armed conflicts before the adoption of Protocol I." That was in 1979. "Therefore, as the Trial Chamber considered Articles 86 and 87 of Protocol I were in this respect only declaring the existing position, and not constituting it. In like manner, the non-reference in Protocol II to command responsibility in relation to internal armed conflicts did not necessarily affect the question whether command responsibility ... existed as part of customary international law relating to internal armed conflicts." If you please go over the page to paragraph 30 where the Appeals Chamber goes on. And they hold: "Were it otherwise, the Appeals Chamber would have to uphold that, 'as argued by the Defence, it is not a crime for a commander in an internal conflict to fail to prevent ... the killings committed by his subordinates ...' The Appeals Chamber does not consider that it is required to sustain so improbable a view in contemporary international law; more particularly, it finds that such a view is not consistent with its reasoning in the Tadic jurisdiction decision the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgment or that of the reasoning of the Trial Chamber in Aleskovski." The Prosecution is mystified as to why this is being raised. What possible -- apart from the fact that law is so clear, it does not matter what sort of armed conflict it is, what possible prejudice could accrue to the accused by not specifying whether it's an internal or international armed conflict? The parties to the conflict were the same. The weapons used were the same. The results were the same. This, in our respectful submission, should be disregarded in its entirety. The Defence has also raised the issue of the body of law which is applicable. Now, this came up at one point during the trial, and Your Honour Judge Liu, Presiding Judge, expressed some surprise when Mr. Mettraux raised the issue of body of law, and Your Honour specifically referred to the Tadic decision. In their brief at paragraph is -- at page 163 on page 504 [sic], the Defence says that "we have not pleaded nor established nor even sought to establish the Geneva Conventions were applicable to this matter other than in relation to the customary image of Common Article 3." Well, that's enough. As the British military -- as the manual of the law of armed conflict, that's the 2004 UK Ministry of Defence law manual says, quote, paragraph 1.13: "When treaty law provisions are declaratory of customary law, the rules they embody are binding on all states even if they are not parties to the treaty concerned. In some cases, a treaty as a whole may be viewed as customary law, while in other cases only certain of a treaty's provisions may be so viewed." Well, the Geneva Conventions, and specifically Common Article 3(1), have attained customary status. Even if it hadn't been adopted in Bosnia in 1992, as it was, it has attained customary status. An indication of that is in the Nicaragua judgement of the International Court of Justice, which is about to be put on to the screen, at paragraph 218. I'll just finish on referring Your Honours to this quote, if that's okay.
