utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this moment I have to remind the Prosecution that they only have 40 minutes to finish their closing argument. So we resume at 3.45 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's continue. Mr. Re, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was just -- before the break, there was just one thing I wanted to refer Your Honours to. Only -- if only to dispose of it, as I hope Your Honours possibly can in your judgement, and that was paragraph 218 of the Nicaragua judgement specifically at paragraph -- page 114 of the ICJ reports where if you could just turn over the page to the second full -- the first full paragraph beginning "Article 3." The line to which I wish to refer Your Honours is the second line which says: "There is no doubt that in the event of international armed conflicts, these rules also constitute a minimum yardstick in addition to the more elaborate rules which also apply in international conflicts." I would very much invite Your Honours to refer to that in the judgement. The part of the respondent -- sorry, the accused's submission to which I am responding at the moment is under the heading 3.5, failure to punish -- prevent and punish the law, which is at pages 5 -- at pages 162 to 163. Paragraph 504, Mr. Halilovic has said: "The Prosecution has not pleaded, has not established, and has in fact not even sought to establish the Geneva Conventions were in force in Bosnia at the time." Now, apart from the fact that -- in fact, on Sanction, if I could have the next one, the Swiss one. Apart from the fact that the ICJ decision and the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision on jurisdiction basically dispose of that argument anyway, refer Your Honours to the document -- it's not in evidence but it doesn't need to be. It's a public document which is from the Swiss government. It's a notification to the governments of the state parties to the Geneva Conventions of 12th of August, 1949 for the protection of war victims. Which states in the first paragraph: "On the 31st December 1992, the Bosnia deposited with the Swiss Federal Council a declaration of succession concerning the four conventions as well as the additional Protocols I and II." It's dated the 17th of February, 1993 It's an open document. Your Honours of course are entitled to refer to it. Now, of course, if I could move to the Tadic judgement, the interlocutory -- sorry, the appeals decision on jurisdiction. I specifically refer Your Honours to paragraphs 132 and 134. And both these sections, and if you look at the middle of paragraph 132 it says: "It should also be noted by a decree, a force of law, that on the 11th of April, 1992, Bosnia adopted the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia," and then refers -- which had of course implemented the two additional protocols of 1977. Then if you go to paragraph 134 the Appeals Chamber expresses a very firm view on the fact that: "Individual criminal responsibility was imposed by virtue of Yugoslavia's ratification of those covenants. So in our submission that is something can be very, very easily disposed of, and perhaps it might even be one of those matters the Defence might like to redact from their final trial brief when they get to it. The next matter which they might possibly like also to redact from their final trial brief is the arguments they put in on levee en masse. I just want to briefly refer Your Honours to the basic authorities. The first one is where it appears, which is Article 4, paragraph 6 of Geneva 3, that's on prisoners of war. And it just says -- it refers to inhabitants of a non-occupied territory, "who on the approach of the enemy spontaneously take up arms to resist the invading forces." If that could be broadcast in Sanction, please. Paragraph 6 of the Geneva Conventions Article -- Geneva 3. Number 2. And the commentary in the Geneva Conventions -- or the ICRC commentary in relation to paragraph 6, en masse levees says this: "The provision is not applicable to inhabitants of the territory who take to the marquis [sic] but only to the mass movements which face the invading forces." This is on page 67 and 68. "With the arms available today, the case is not likely to arise in the open country side but it is more probable in the built-up area where even the rudimentary methods are of some value." Now, the crucial part of this commentary is page 68 of the commentary, which I'm sure is coming up on our screen any second. It should, however, be emphasised that mass levee can only be considered to exist during a very short period, that is during the actual invasion period. If resistance continues, the authority commanding the inhabitants would have taken up arms or the authority to which they profess allegiance must either replace them by sending regular units or incorporate them into its regular forces. Otherwise the mass levee could not survive the total occupation of the territory which it has tried in vain to defend." The -- again, these matters have both been referred to in more detail by my colleagues. I'm just pointing Your Honours to the law. And the Prosecution just simply invites the Trial Chamber to if it remains in the brief after redaction to dismiss it in a line or two. There is simply no evidence whatsoever of a levee en masse. The next argument I turn to in the Defence's brief which in the Prosecution's submission is basically wrong in law, and I ask for Sanction to display paragraph 77 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision which is document 5, is that of causality. That appears at pages 189 and 190 of the brief. Paragraphs 587 through 589 at which the Defence submits that the Defence's position under customary international law is that "it requires a causal link between the failure and the crimes or consequences thereof." Unfortunately, the Defence have quoted no supporting authority to support this, we say, rather bold assertion that causality is required. The only authorities we can find in our researches, an article by Otto Trivtera [phoen] four years ago and mentioned by learned co-counsel, Mr. Mettraux, in his own book. And the Prosecution submits that mention in one article and one book cannot make -- cannot transform this into a doctrine of customary international law, and especially not retrospectively. I refer you to paragraph 77 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement, which is referred to at paragraph at 589 and footnote 1214 where the Appellant -- sorry, why did I say Appellant? The accused, I'm sorry, submitted that Blaskic said that the Appeals Chamber "was not satisfied persuaded by the Appellant's submission on the existence of causality" between a commander's failure and the crimes of his subordinates. Unfortunately, Your Honours can see when the full quote is put up before you on the screen in front of you that the full story is something completely different. The quote reads: "The Appeals Chamber is therefore not persuaded by the Appellant's submission that the existence of causality between a commander's failure to prevent subordinates' crimes and the occurrence of these crimes is an element of command responsibility that requires proof by the Prosecution in all circumstances," in all circumstances, "of a case." And the next line is a crucial one which was omitted from the Defence brief. "Once again, it is more a question of fact to be established on a case-by-case basis than a question of law in general." That's, in our respectful submission, is and has to be the law, and Your Honours can very, very easily dispose of that argument if it survives the editing process. The next one I refer to is the argument of acquiescence which is at page 199 and paragraph 616 of the brief at which the Defence again bravely and boldly assert that the Prosecution has failed to establish any failure that might be attributable to Mr. Halilovic that would have been intentional and deliberate so as to amount to acquiescence on the part -- on his part of the crimes charged as required by Article 7(3). Again, this is something for which it is absolutely devoid of any authority, opinion juris, state practice, customary law to support this assertion that acquiescence is required to establish command responsibility. The Prosecution submits the position is clear that no endorsement is indeed necessary. The international humanitarian law imposes positive duties on commanders, a breach of which can result in criminal liability. And if you were to accept this argument it would basically transform it into a charge under Article 7(1). It is very similar to that of causality. Another argument which -- or another section or part of the Defence brief which again is just wrong is at page 131 at paragraph 412. In that particular paragraph, learned Defence counsel express their "most serious reservations" as to whether back in 19 -- September 1993 customary law could have supported the conviction of command for any special intent crimes committed by his subordinates where he did not himself possess or share that special mens rea." That's wrong in law for several reasons. First the Appeals Chamber has quite distinctly decided that it does in the Krnojelac decision. And secondly, the crime charged here, murder, is not a special or specific intent crime. There are only three; that's genocide, persecution, and torture, and murder isn't one of those. That's another argument or section, entire section which the Trial Chamber should have no difficulty in dismissing outright. Another argument which I wish to refer to in passing is page 24 which is paragraph 80 of the Defence brief where the Defence attack the Prosecution under the heading of Prosecution's failure to seek to identify the perpetrators of the crime and at paragraph 79 and 80 make a great deal of the fact that the Prosecution did not attempt to show photographs to a witness in an attempt to have the witness identify the perpetrators. Well, what's wrong with that particular submission? What is wrong with it is it would be absurd, ludicrous, it would be an -- apart from the unreliability of photographic evidence generally, of identification evidence, the Defence cannot seriously be suggesting that years after the event we would be showing someone who was of very, very tender years at the time, witnessing something very, very traumatic, photographs to assist them in ascertaining the identity of someone who has already come to the Tribunal to give evidence. There is not a shred of doubt as to who killed the family of that witness. The Trial Chamber has heard direct evidence of that. And the Defence even concedes the deaths of those people in its brief as breaches of international humanitarian law and by members of the 9th Brigade. Again, that is something which the Trial Chamber should have no difficulty, in our submission, in dismissing outright. I'd also like to move now to Blaskic paragraph 22 -- sorry, paragraph 62, if we could move to that one. Another argument which is wrong is at paragraph 409 of the Defence brief where the -- I'm sorry. 403, my apologies. Page 127 where the Defence say, the bottom of the paragraph: "It is therefore not sufficient that the commander knows in general terms that the crimes have or may be about to be committed by his subordinates." The reason why that is wrong in law is that the Blaskic Appeals Chamber has set out at paragraph 62 of its judgement that -- I won't read the whole thing. I'll just put it in front of Your Honours and you can see it, in the interests of time. Your Honours can see from the paragraph which is listed there that there is absolutely no requirement suggested that the -- a commander should know in general terms about what -- what crimes had been -- that it was not sufficient that they knew in general terms the crime had been committed. The question is whether or not the person had the knowledge which puts them on notice. It's nothing to do with generality. It amounts very much to the specifics of the circumstances, and it must be decided on a case-by-case basis. Another suggestion in the Defence brief we wish to basically rebut is that at paragraph 560 on page 179 where the Defence suggests that somehow the Prosecution is suggesting that Mr. Halilovic should have been in charge of the investigation and taken all sorts of measures such as interviews, on-sight visits, exhumations, et cetera, look, we'll put this down on the part of the Defence as rhetoric. We have never suggested that. We certainly don't suggest that the Chief of Staff, the commander of an operation, should personally go down on to the ground and do all the things that investigators, trained investigators, should be doing. Mr. Halilovic's duties were quite clear. There is no suggestion that he should have been personally in charge of taking fingerprints or digging up bodies or anything like that. Another issue which has been touched upon in the Defence brief is that of mistake of law where the Defence is suggesting at page 168, that's paragraph 521 of the brief, that this may well operate in Mr. Halilovic's case and it's something that the Prosecution may well have to negative. Mr. Halilovic of course, in his book which is Exhibit 281 at page 6, himself basically overrides any suggestion that he could have been suffering from any mistake of law if indeed it could apply where he said: "That is why I personally found the stains on the Bosnian consciousness, such as the murders of the FRYs in Funista [phoen], the Oristovic [phoen] case, the events in Uzdol and the Grabovica case that much more difficult to take was precisely because of this that I insisted on upholding law and order, which in my view requires a thorough investigation and detection in judicial punishment of the perpetrators." For the most recent statement that we can find of mistake of law is put on the screen very briefly firstly Cassese's International Criminal Law. This is paragraph 13.4. If Your Honours can just see the very bottom, the last paragraph: "It is submitted that mistake of law may be pleaded as a valid excuse not when the offender was unaware of the unlawfulness but when: (i) he had no knowledge of an essential element of law referred to in the international prohibition of a certain conduct;

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: consequently the person, when he took a certain action did not possess the requisite mens rea." Please put the next one up which is from the British manual. We clearly submit that known of those three elements identified by Cassese could possibly be applicable in this particular case, especially when Mr. Halilovic himself in the Defence submission says that after the event, even if it might have been years after the event, was demanding an investigation into the event. And in his inspection team report was indeed demanding the replacement of certain commanders for various infractions. If you turn to the latest authority which we can find on this particular area, ignorance of the law, we direct Your Honours to paragraph 16.43, and this is the UK military manual which says: "Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but if the law is unclear or controversial, an accused should be given the benefit of that lack of clarity by the award of a lesser or nominal punishment." Again, that is something which just does not apply here. I'd also refer Your Honours to two specific exhibits in this regard, and that is Exhibit P103, which is the decree relating to the implementation of the international laws of war in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and specifically paragraphs 1 and 2. That was as Your Honours will recall President Izetbegovic's decree of the 23rd of August, 1992, stating that the armed forces of the republic will implement the international laws of war, including international conventions and treaties, Geneva Conventions, of course, customary international law, general principles of international law of war, and its publication of course in the army gazette on the 5th of December, 1992, which is Exhibit P104. And paragraph 2 states: "The parties to the conflict bear responsibility for grave breaches for international -- of international law of war no matter how the principles of law are violated," and so on. It would be inconceivable that Mr. Halilovic, an experienced JNA officer, well-versed in the laws of war as part of his training and indeed the Chief of Staff and the person whom the Defence are keen to put forward as one who attempted to do everything he could to ensure the laws of war were obeyed in Bosnia was not aware of the duties of a commander under international humanitarian law. I turn to the two -- the failures to prevent in Grabovica and Uzdol. Firstly, Grabovica. The Prosecution submits that the evidence has very clearly established that Mr. Halilovic received actual notice, at least on the evening of the 9th of September, 1993. Now, of course the Defence has made complaint again about what the indictment says, but as we said at the very beginning of the case when Your Honour asked -- Your Honour Judge Liu asked questions, all we can say is there may be conflicting evidence as to dates and times, and it is what is established by the evidence at the end of the case that is important. The accused has been on notice that we say he was informed of -- received actual notice of the crimes very soon afterwards. The evidence in indeed his own book makes it quite clear that this was on the very earliest the 9th of September, 1993. That's 1993. And that of course was the very day on which the murders were still occurring. Now, I digress for a moment here. Another point in the Defence brief is that we plead that the murders occurred on the morning but the evidence show that some of them were still occurring in the afternoon. Again, we say, Well -- the trouble -- I mean, evidence never comes completely up to -- never completely follows an indictment. It cannot. You have to allow for the vagaries of memory and people giving their evidence as to times and places. In any event, it makes no difference in our submission whether Your Honours find the murders continued into the afternoon or finished on the morning of the 9th of September. The issue here is when Mr. Halilovic found out. The evidence is fairly clear that he had to have found out on the 9th, the day of the murders. Having done so, he had a duty to take reasonable and necessary measures. And of course as we've already outlined, these must be decided on a case-by-case basis, and there's no definition of what he could or should have done; it depends very much on the circumstances. The evidence has established that as the commander of the inspection team and of the forces in the area at the time, he had the material ability, he had military police at his disposal, there were two platoons, the 6th Corps, which he could have utilised. District military courts were operating. At the very minimum he should have ordered a proper investigation. He should have ordered the military police to assist. He should have ordered that military police be co-opted. He should have ordered the crime scene secured. He should have reported the crime to his commander, that's Delic, and sought all assistance necessary to do all of those things, to ensure that the perpetrators were punished. Mr. Halilovic knew on the 9th of the September who the likely perpetrators were; everyone did. Everyone in Jablanica knew it was the troops from Sarajevo, the very people who Mr. Halilovic had brought there. Instead of doing what he should have done, he gave Mr. Dzankovic only the vaguest of orders and that was orally and that was only once and without any follow-up at all. This, in the Prosecution's submission, constitutes a clear breach of his duties to punish. As a result of his only asking Mr. Dzankovic in the vaguest possible terms to find out what had happened, the Prosecution has established that no proper investigation was carried out by anyone in military security or the inspection team, there were no attempts made, no proper attempts were made to secure the crime scene, no attempts were made to interview eyewitnesses or any of the perpetrators. And it wouldn't have been hard, and you've heard the evidence, to find out exactly who those people were. No members of the units possibly responsible for the murders were interviewed. The evidence was no one was interviewed until 1998. No forensic investigation was performed, and the evidence was the bodies were still there weeks later with skulls and bones sticking out of the ground, and the smell was so great that concern was raised that they should go -- people should go and cover them up. No attempts were made to arrest the perpetrators, and again it would not have been hard to find out who they were. No one was given the task of overseeing the investigation, and that was Mr. Halilovic's role, to give someone the task of overseeing the investigation and to ensure that it was followed through. No formal lines of responsibility for investigating were ever put in place. The military did not formally request assistance from the civilian police. And as Your Honours are aware, no one was actually apprehended until many, many years later. Most of those responsible for the crimes have never been prosecuted, never brought to justice. The only two who have been prosecuted were Mr. Sakrak, who gave evidence here, and Mr. Bahota [phoen]. And that's it. Clearly many more members of the 9th Brigade were involved, and it would not have been difficult to find out who they were, either then on the day, or in the days or weeks afterwards. But, and this goes -- this goes to Mr. Halilovic's mens rea. Knowing of the involvement of members of the 9th Brigade in the massacres, these gravest of war crimes in Grabovica, what did he do? Showing his attitude to how he viewed troops under his command committing massacres of civilians, once they went back to Sarajevo he didn't order -- ask for them to be arrested or segregated there or be investigated there, no; he actually ordered their return -- Celo and his men ordered their return - and Caco - back to Herzegovina on the 24th of September, 1994. While others in the supreme command were planning the arrest of Celo and Caco, Mr. Halilovic was planning to use them again in combat. The only inference in totality of this is that Mr. Halilovic wanted just to ignore what had happened in Grabovica; he was not interested. He did not want to investigate. He did not care. He just wanted to put it all behind him and get on with the combat in Herzegovina. To allow this to happen cuts across the very heart of international humanitarian law. Immediate measures must be taken to punish the perpetrators of grave crimes against civilians. And knowing what his subordinates had done in Grabovica, that gave Mr. Halilovic added inquiry notice that the moment he heard that anything similar might have happened in relation to other soldiers under his command, he had an added impetus to do something to take immediate action, and that is exactly what he should have done in Uzdol. Now, the Trial Chamber is entitled to use the same evidence of command and control in relation to Grabovica, the orders of issuing orders to subordinates who obeyed them, the Neretva map which is to my side there showing the scope and the size of the operation, the fact that he issued orders directly including those to Enver Buza. You're entitled to use all of that to find that the Prozor Independent Battalion was directly subordinated to Mr. Halilovic at the time they committed these gravest of war crimes. And if so, he had a duty to punish their criminality. The evidence shows that Mr. Halilovic found out within days that the allegations -- it wouldn't have been difficult to find that out either. They were broadcast around the world. Kate Adie broadcast it on the 15th, the day afterwards. As Witness J said, people were talking about it or not talking about it. It was obvious something had happened. It was being broadcast in the Croatian media. Mr. Halilovic could not have not known what was alleged to have happened in Uzdol by very virtue of the fact that he was there; but there's positive evidence that he found out about it within days. What did he do about it? Well, the evidence establishes that he did nothing about it. Dzankovic who he tasked in the vaguest possible way to look into what had happened at Grabovica didn't even know about it until he returned to Sarajevo. He 6th Corps military police weren't utilised. Eminovic from the 6th Corps wasn't properly -- wasn't utilised. The evidence was that there wasn't any sort of investigation at all. Witness J's evidence, at best, was incoherent but at worst was of nothing more than a whitewash or a cover-up by Enver Buza which is reflected in his report which went all the way up to the supreme command and was adopted even by Mr. Jasarevic on its way to the presidency. Our submission is that the only inference from the totality of the evidence available is that Mr. Halilovic as the commander of the soldiers in Grabovica did absolutely nothing to punish their criminality. A miscellaneous matter I wish to refer the Trial Chamber to is the Defence submissions at pages 700 -- sorry, paragraph 770 of the brief onwards. It's under the -- page 240, paragraph 770 to 784. In the Prosecution's submission, there are -- the Defence has stooped to a new low in some of the submissions they have made there, particularly at paragraph 779 when they refer to the conduct of the investigation and related matters. And once again, they have reared the bogeyman of Mr. Nikolai Mikhailov and alleged that he and another Prosecution officer were fired from this office. At the moment that matter is a matter of litigation in the Appeals Chamber, where the Prosecution has asked the Appeals Chamber to direct the Defence to redact those allegations, those unsourced and untrue allegations from the appeal brief they filed. That matter is awaiting determination. In the Prosecution's submission, these allegations form no part of the case. They should not be in this brief. We will be filing ourselves a motion to strike them from the brief in writing within the next few days. And we ask the Trial Chamber to disregard these in their entirety and also to disregard the allegations put in these vague and couched terms at paragraph 782 of mysterious disappearances of things from the Prosecution archives and no less mysterious was the floor translation and so on. These form no part of proper, civilised legal discourse. These matters have all been properly answered. They should not rear their ugly heads yet again at the end of the Defence final trial brief. The last paragraph is 784: "The above matter is a very serious one insofar as it might constitute an abuse of process-- of the process. The Trial Chamber should carefully consider evidence suggesting misconduct on the part of Mr. Mikhailov." Our response to that is, well, if the Defence wish to bring an allegation of abuse of process they should do so. They should file an motion before the relevant body alleging contempt or abuse of process and not just make these throw-away allegations at the very end to contaminate, pollute, in our submission, the minds of the Trial Chamber. This should be completely disregarded. The -- I won't address at any length at all on the matters of sentencing Mr. Halilovic. The Prosecution submits that we have established beyond reasonable doubt the following. The 9th and 10th Brigades had committed numerous crimes against the civilian population in Sarajevo in 1993. Mr. Halilovic was well aware of their reputation and the crimes committed by these brigades. In August 1993 he was appointed to lead an inspection team with authority to command combat in Herzegovina; that's Operation Neretva. As the commander of the team he subordinated units to his command. He issued orders that the units subordinated obeyed. He ordered that soldiers of the 9th and the 10th be subordinated to him in Operation Neretva. Soldiers of the 9th were billeted and accommodated with Bosnian Croat civilians in Grabovica. Mr. Halilovic took no steps to prevent these soldiers from committing crimes against those civilians. On the 8th and 9th of September, 1993, the soldiers murdered 27 Bosnian Croat civilians. Mr. Halilovic was notified of the crimes on the 9th, and he knew by that day that it was most likely the 9th who had committed the crimes. Knowing that, he failed to have the crimes properly investigated or punished. We've also established that on the 13th of September, 1993, he ordered personally the Prozor Independent Battalion, subordinated to his command, to attack the HVO-held village of Uzdol. The following day in the course of the combat, members of the Prozor Independent Battalion murdered 29 Bosnian Croat civilians. And finally the Prosecution has established that Mr. Halilovic took no steps at all to have those crimes investigated and the perpetrators punished while the soldiers remain subordinated to his command, and indeed no one has ever been prosecuted to these days -- to this day. The Prosecution submits that it has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the only verdict available to the Trial Chamber is one of guilt. The appropriate sentence, we submit, in all of the circumstances is one of ten years of imprisonment. We take no issue with any of the matters raised in mitigation by Mr. Halilovic in his brief. The matters are all properly pleaded and referred to in his brief. But having said that, ten years is the appropriate sentence, and we ask is the Trial Chamber to convict the accused and to sentence him to ten years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Mr. Weiner, do you have anything to add at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour. That's our case. You told us three and a half hours. We went three hours and 26 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since there's a lot of works of authorities cited during your closing argument, could I ask whether you are going to file the book of authorities at this stage? Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Most of them are ICTY judgements. We will certainly file the other authorities we've referred to. If Your Honours want the ICRC commentary, we can file that, but definitely the other ones we'll file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that you mentioned, for instance, Professor Cassese's book of international criminal law as well as the latest publication of the distinguished Defence counsel. But if so, I believe that you have to file it. Only indicate the page number or paragraph number rather than the whole context. We want a kind of catalogue document rather than all the contents, because we could find them easily in the library or in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much indeed. Well -- and if you -- when do you think you would be ready to file it? How about within this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly. The only reason why we haven't done it before was of course we're responding to arguments in the Defence brief, those particular matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may file it within a week's time. Well, there are two matters that I would like to hear the parties. The first issue is about the Defence motion for the admission of the exhibit, that is MFI 221 which was filed on the 12th of August. Could we ask the Prosecution to respond to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there's no objections, this document is admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. The next issue is about Prosecution's motion to admit Sefer Halilovic's letter to President Izetbegovic on the 1st of May, 1995, into evidence, filed on the 29th August. Are there any objections on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are none. That document reflects almost word-for-word Exhibit P281, the Halilovic book. And Your Honour will observe that comparing the two documents, one seems to be based on the other. So we don't object to that being tendered now and that's what we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. This document is admitted into the evidence. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could I raise one other potential exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very recently material was provided to the Defence. We've given that to the Prosecutor. We've asked them to give us an indication as to whether they would oppose it being admitted. It's very late to do this, but it's a small document. The Prosecutor indicated a general position about it that was favourable but hasn't committed to it yet, and I don't think I should demand an answer now. But can I just indicate that tomorrow morning it may be that we -- perhaps I don't need --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I can make it much quicker. No objection to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to inform me which document so the registrar could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wonder if that could be done first thing tomorrow morning. I don't know that I have a -- I had a copy of it and I wrote inadvertently all over it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Therefore, perhaps if we could formally deal with that matter tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And another issue is that the Prosecution filed a motion for the provisional release of Mr. Halilovic. I wonder whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Defence did that. The Prosecution didn't file any motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. I'm sorry about that. I wonder if the Prosecution is in the position to make a reply orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I spoke with Madam del Ponte today, the Prosecutor, and it is her view that as a matter of office policy after a case has been completed but prior to a judgement being issued, our office will oppose all requests for provisional release. It is her view that it is at that time, prior to judgement, that a defendant would most likely disappear or flee from the jurisdiction or flee and go into hiding. As a result, it is her view and it's her policy, it's the policy of the office, that we oppose any requests for provisional release at that time. It was further the view that recently a number of cases have -- a number of Chambers have allowed provisional release in various situations. And we are an International Tribunal, the world is watching and the world is watching the type of justice that is going on here. And it is the view of the office that it is improper -- I shouldn't -- actually -- improper, it's not the right choice that is being taken to allow people to -- allow defendants to leave prior to the judgement. It is the view that the public is watching and the public sees people charged with very serious crimes and they see these people are just being released. And what it does is the Tribunal loses the confidence of the public with such action. So as I said, I have spoken with the Prosecutor today, and she has requested that I recommend to this Court that the request for provisional release be opposed and that it be denied on those bases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, suppose this Trial Chamber grants the motion by the Defence for the provisional release. Could I regard your submission as a request for delay of the execution of that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Under the latest view of the Appeals Court, there's no longer a need for the delay, you can appeal directly. It's not longer required that we request a stay pending -- pending a hearing -- a request to leave from the Appeals Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it's not necessary, if that's what the Court wishes. However, once again, it's our request that not only do you delay -- should you delay allowing him provisional release but that you refuse to grant his request for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, any other matters? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, no other matters arising out of that. I take it Prosecutor have put forward a policy position, and it's correct for them to communicate a policy position to you if that's the way they see it. It didn't relate to Mr. Halilovic personally directly in any way. Other than that, Your Honours, we will be ready to proceed tomorrow. We don't have Sanction. We'll provide some -- some printed copies of exhibits that are in the case, but we'll also provide the reference of those so that they'll be uploaded in the e-court system, and we'll give a copy to the Prosecutors, of course. I undertake to finish within time. And, Your Honours, I just wanted to ask if -- I'm sorry to trouble the Tribunal with this. But currently I have the personal commitment to fly home to my family the following day, and I wonder -- I understood that the position was that we would complete the reply -- such responses, as they have to be, that we would complete those tomorrow as well.
